questions.title: Deadlock Storm Under Load: Root Cause and Prevention
questions.prompt: Your OLTP system is throwing an increasing number of deadlock errors (1205) during peak hours, and the on-call team's current fix is just to retry the failed transaction. As the architect, walk through: what a deadlock actually is at the lock-manager level, why SQL Server resolves it by picking a victim, and the concrete, durable design changes you'd make to drive the deadlock rate toward zero rather than just making retries cheaper.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a circular wait: Transaction A holds a lock Transaction B needs, while B simultaneously holds a lock A needs, so neither can ever proceed without intervention. SQL Server's lock monitor periodically scans for exactly this cycle and, once found, picks a 'victim' to roll back automatically, based on which transaction is cheaper to undo (or an explicit DEADLOCK_PRIORITY setting), raising error 1205 to the victim's caller. Retrying the rolled-back transaction only treats the symptom — it does nothing to reduce how often the cycle forms in the first place. The durable fixes are architectural: (1) enforce a consistent access order to tables across every code path that touches them, since the single most common real-world cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; (2) keep transactions as short as possible, moving validation and unrelated reads outside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary so locks are held for the minimum necessary time; (3) review indexing so transactions acquire narrow row/page locks instead of escalating to page or table locks on large scans, which dramatically widens the blast radius of any single transaction; (4) consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation, which removes most reader/writer blocking entirely via row versioning, at the cost of additional tempdb version-store overhead; (5) for cases where natural ordering genuinely can't be enforced, use sp_getapplock to serialize access explicitly. Before declaring any fix complete, capture an actual deadlock graph (via Extended Events' xml_deadlock_report) to confirm the real access pattern rather than guessing from symptoms.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team, respectfully, that retrying is a band-aid, not a fix — it just hides the real cost of the problem. First I'd pull an actual deadlock graph, not just the error count, because I want to see exactly which two statements and which two resources are colliding before I propose anything. Nine times out of ten it comes down to two code paths touching the same tables in opposite order, so step one is standardizing access order across every stored procedure that touches those tables. Step two is auditing transaction length — anything that's validating data or doing unrelated reads inside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary comes out. Then I look at whether lock escalation is widening the blast radius because of missing indexes, and only after that do I bring up snapshot isolation as a structural option, being upfront that it moves the cost into tempdb rather than eliminating it. I'd present this as 'here's the mechanism, here's the evidence, here's what actually gets the rate toward zero' rather than just 'add a try/catch and retry.'
commonMistakes: Treats retry logic as the fix instead of eliminating the cause
Doesn't look at actual access order across stored procedures
Ignores lock escalation thresholds on large updates
Assumes deadlocks are a bug SQL Server should prevent rather than a resolvable mutual-wait
Never captures an actual deadlock graph (XML) before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Defines deadlock as a circular wait on locks, not a generic error
Explains SQL Server's victim-selection mechanism
Identifies inconsistent access order as the most common root cause
Proposes shortening transactions and reviewing indexing to reduce lock footprint
Considers snapshot isolation as an architectural lever, with its tradeoff (tempdb/version store)
Recommends instrumentation (deadlock graph / extended events) before declaring a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains deadlock mechanics and victim selection

questions.title: Choosing a Clustering Key for a High-Volume Staging Table
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a junior developer's design for a staging table that receives 20 million new rows per night via SSIS, and is then read heavily by downstream MERGE statements keyed on a natural composite business key (OrderID, LineNumber). They clustered the table on that natural composite key because 'that's what we query by.' As the architect, do you approve this design? Walk through the tradeoffs and give the clustering strategy you'd actually recommend, with DDL.
questions.modelAnswer: I would not approve this as-is. A good clustering key is narrow, unique, and ever-increasing, because every nonclustered index on the table silently carries the clustering key as its row pointer, and an ever-increasing key means new rows append at the end instead of forcing page splits. A two-column natural business key fails two of those three tests: it's wide (bloating every nonclustered index on this table), and even though OrderID trends upward, concurrent SSIS data flow buffers inserting in parallel won't guarantee strict insertion order against that composite key, which causes fragmentation and page splits under 20M-rows/night load. The fix is to separate 'what the physical order should optimize for' from 'what enforces the business rule': add a narrow, ever-increasing surrogate (an IDENTITY BIGINT) as the clustering key, so inserts are fast and append-only, and enforce the business key's uniqueness and support the MERGE lookup pattern with a nonclustered unique index on (OrderID, LineNumber), with the columns the MERGE actually needs included to keep it covering. At this volume, I'd also suggest a LoadBatchID column and considering partitioning or at least batch-based purging, since clustering on an ever-increasing surrogate also makes truncating/reloading by batch cheap.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on this gently but firmly. The instinct makes sense — 'we query by it, so cluster on it' — but at 20 million rows a night that composite key doesn't give me the one thing I actually need from a clustering key: guaranteed append-only insert order. I'd walk through why: every nonclustered index on this table is carrying that two-column key as baggage, and under concurrent SSIS inserts I'm going to see fragmentation creep in even though OrderID itself trends upward. My recommendation is to split the concerns — a narrow surrogate IDENTITY as the clustering key purely for insert performance, and a unique nonclustered index on the business key to both enforce uniqueness and serve the downstream MERGE. I'd show them the DDL side by side so it's concrete, not abstract, and I'd flag that at this scale I also want to talk about batch-based purging so we're not fighting fragmentation and bloat at the same time.
questions.example:
CREATE TABLE stg.OrderLineStaging (
    StagingID BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    OrderID INT NOT NULL,
    LineNumber SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    ProductID INT NOT NULL,
    OrderQty INT NOT NULL,
    UnitPrice MONEY NOT NULL,
    LoadBatchID INT NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_OrderLineStaging PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED (StagingID)
);
GO

CREATE UNIQUE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_OrderLineStaging_BusinessKey
ON stg.OrderLineStaging (OrderID, LineNumber)
INCLUDE (ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice);
GO

-- Downstream MERGE seeks this nonclustered index instead of scanning
MERGE INTO dbo.FactOrderLine AS tgt
USING stg.OrderLineStaging AS src
    ON tgt.OrderID = src.OrderID AND tgt.LineNumber = src.LineNumber
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET tgt.OrderQty = src.OrderQty, tgt.UnitPrice = src.UnitPrice
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (OrderID, LineNumber, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice)
    VALUES (src.OrderID, src.LineNumber, src.ProductID, src.OrderQty, src.UnitPrice);

Ignores that every nonclustered index silently carries the clustering key
Doesn't consider insert-order fragmentation under high-volume parallel loads
Forgets the business key still needs uniqueness enforcement somewhere
Never proposes partitioning/batch purging for a staging table at this volume
keyPoints: Recommends a narrow ever-increasing surrogate clustering key for heavy insert workloads
Preserves the business key as a nonclustered unique index for MERGE lookups
Explains the nonclustered-index pointer-width tradeoff
Considers partitioning/batching for fast purge at 20M-rows/night scale
Backs the recommendation with concrete DDL

questions.title: A Report That Used to Run in Seconds Now Times Out
questions.prompt: A monthly sales report query against a now-50-million-row fact table has quietly gone from 2 seconds to over 3 minutes as the table grew. Nobody changed the query. Explain, at an architect level, the full diagnostic sequence you'd run to find the cause, the category of root causes you'd expect at this scale, and show the SARGable rewrite for the single most common offender you'd check first.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd run a fixed sequence, not guess. First, turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and look for a scan where a seek should be, and for a large gap between estimated and actual row counts, which flags stale statistics. Second, capture a baseline with SET STATISTICS IO and TIME ON so I have real logical-reads and CPU numbers before touching anything. Third, audit every WHERE and JOIN predicate for non-SARGable patterns — a function wrapping a column, an implicit data-type conversion, or a leading wildcard — because this is the single most common cause of a query that 'used to be fine' degrading purely from table growth: a full scan that was negligible at a few hundred thousand rows becomes minutes of work at 50 million, with nothing about the query's logic having changed. Fourth, check statistics freshness directly via sys.dm_db_stats_properties, since the auto-update threshold scales with table size and large tables can go a long time between automatic updates. Fifth, consider parameter sniffing if the query is parameterized and a plan cached for an atypical parameter value is now being reused for typical ones. In this scenario the leading suspect is almost always a non-SARGable date predicate, which I'd rewrite as a range against the untouched column.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never start by guessing or by reaching for 'let's just add an index.' I turn on the actual plan first and look for a scan where I'd expect a seek, and I check the gap between estimated and actual rows, because that gap alone often tells me stale statistics are at least part of the story. Then I capture STATISTICS IO and TIME so I have a real before number, because I want to prove any fix afterward, not just feel like it's faster. At that point I go straight to the predicates — in my experience, a function wrapped around a column or an implicit conversion is the single most common reason a query that used to be fine quietly degrades as a table grows past tens of millions of rows, because the cost of a full scan scales with the table even though nothing in the query text changed. I'd show the before-and-after rewrite side by side so it's obvious the fix is removing the function from the column, not adding an index that a wrapped predicate wouldn't even use.
questions.example:
-- Non-SARGable (the likely offender)
SELECT SUM(f.SalesAmount)
FROM dbo.FactInternetSales AS f
JOIN dbo.DimDate AS d ON d.DateKey = f.OrderDateKey
WHERE YEAR(d.FullDateAlternateKey) = 2013;

-- SARGable rewrite: untouched column, range comparison
DECLARE @StartDate DATE = '2013-01-01', @EndDate DATE = '2014-01-01';

SELECT SUM(f.SalesAmount)
FROM dbo.FactInternetSales AS f
JOIN dbo.DimDate AS d ON d.DateKey = f.OrderDateKey
WHERE d.FullDateAlternateKey >= @StartDate AND d.FullDateAlternateKey < @EndDate;
commonMistakes: Jumps straight to 'add an index' without checking the plan first
Doesn't establish a STATISTICS IO/TIME baseline before changing anything
Overlooks stale statistics as a cause distinct from bad predicates
Assumes the query degraded because 'the server is slow' instead of profiling
Adds an index without removing the non-SARGable wrapper that prevents the index from being used anyway
keyPoints: Lays out a repeatable diagnostic sequence: plan, STATISTICS IO/TIME, predicate audit, stats freshness
Identifies non-SARGable predicates as the most common cause at scale
Produces a correct SARGable rewrite
Explains why the same predicate 'got worse' purely from table growth
Mentions parameter sniffing/stale stats as secondary suspects

Correctly identifies non-SARGable predicates as the leading cause at scale
Provides a correct, working SARGable rewrite
Covers secondary causes (stats, parameter sniffing)

questions.title: Reporting Queries Are Blocking the Nightly Order Pipeline
questions.prompt: Business users running ad-hoc reports against the live OLTP database during business hours are intermittently blocking order-entry transactions, and vice versa. Compare the architectural options — read-committed snapshot isolation, a reporting replica, and query hints like NOLOCK — and recommend what you'd actually implement, including what you give up.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, readers take shared locks and writers take exclusive locks, so reports and order-entry transactions genuinely contend for the same locks on the same rows, causing exactly this symptom. NOLOCK (or READ UNCOMMITTED) removes that blocking by skipping locking entirely, but it allows dirty reads, can double-count or miss rows during a page split, and is unacceptable for anything a finance or operations team relies on for correctness — I would not recommend it as a general answer here. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), enabled at the database level, gives readers a transactionally consistent versioned snapshot from tempdb's version store instead of taking shared locks, so reporting reads stop blocking writers and vice versa, with zero application code changes for ordinary SELECTs — the cost is additional tempdb space and I/O for the version store, and a small per-row overhead on writers. A reporting replica (an Always On readable secondary, log shipping, or replication) solves a different, broader problem: it isolates the reporting workload's CPU and I/O consumption from the OLTP instance entirely, not just lock contention, at the cost of replication lag and additional infrastructure to maintain. My recommendation: enable RCSI first as the fast, low-risk fix for the specific symptom described (lock contention), and treat a readable secondary as the real architectural answer once the reporting workload itself starts consuming OLTP compute/I/O capacity, not just locks. The two aren't mutually exclusive — a mature design often has both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different problems that look the same from the outside: lock contention, and resource contention. For the immediate symptom — reports and order entry fighting over row locks — I'd recommend turning on read-committed snapshot isolation. It lets readers work off a versioned snapshot instead of taking shared locks, so the blocking just stops, and it needs no code changes. I'd be upfront that it's not free — it adds load to tempdb's version store — but that's a much safer tradeoff than reaching for NOLOCK, which I'd actually argue against here, because dirty reads on order data are a real correctness risk, not just a theoretical one. If the real issue turns out to be that reporting is also eating CPU and I/O the OLTP system needs, that's a different conversation — that's when I'd bring in a readable secondary, because RCSI doesn't give you more hardware, it just removes lock contention. I'd frame it to the client as 'quick structural fix now, workload separation as the next step if reporting keeps growing.'

Doesn't distinguish lock contention from resource (CPU/IO) contention
Treats RCSI as free, ignoring tempdb version-store cost
Proposes a replica without acknowledging replication lag implications for 'real-time' reports

questions.title: Promoting an SSIS Project Across Dev, Test, and Production Safely
questions.prompt: A client has one SSIS project that needs to run correctly against three SQL Server environments (Dev, Test, Prod) with different connection strings and file paths, promoted through the pipeline without ever hand-editing a package. Explain the SSIS Catalog mechanism that makes this possible, the one hard constraint you must design around, and how you'd structure environments and references for a clean promotion process.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the project deployment model, an entire SSIS project — every package plus its parameters — builds into one .ispac file and deploys as a single unit to the SSISDB catalog. SSISDB's Environments feature solves the per-environment-value problem: an environment is a named container of variables (Dev, Test, Production) created within a catalog folder, and a project's parameters or connection manager properties get mapped, via 'Use environment variable,' to pull their actual value from whichever environment is active for a given execution. The same deployed binary runs unchanged; only the resolved values differ. The hard constraint to design around: a single package execution can reference only one environment — you cannot mix Dev and Production variables in the same run, which is also the deliberate safety rail preventing a half-dev, half-prod execution by accident. For a clean promotion process, I'd deploy the identical .ispac to each environment's own SSISDB folder (or a shared catalog with per-environment folders), create a matching environment per folder with environment-appropriate values and secrets marked Sensitive (encrypted via the catalog's master key), and have each SQL Agent job step's Configuration tab reference the environment matching its own server. The deployment itself should be scripted (via the Deployment Wizard's command-line mode or catalog stored procedures) rather than done by hand, so promotion is repeatable and auditable, and the project's source-controlled parameter defaults never get hand-edited post-deploy.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanism that makes this work is the project deployment model plus environments. I deploy one .ispac — the whole project, built once — and I never touch it per environment. Instead, I set up an Environment per target, each with its own variables, and map the project's parameters to 'use environment variable' instead of a fixed default. The one rule I always flag to a client up front is that an execution can only pull from one environment at a time — that's actually a feature, because it's what makes it structurally impossible to accidentally run a job against production data using a dev connection string. For promotion itself, I insist on scripting the deployment — same artifact, same steps, every environment — because the moment someone hand-edits a connection string in Prod 'just this once,' you've lost the whole benefit of this model. I also make sure every secret in those environments is marked Sensitive so it's encrypted at rest under the catalog's master key, and I keep a backup of that master key, because losing it means you can't move the catalog to a new instance.
commonMistakes: Doesn't realize an execution can only pull from one environment
Proposes editing connection strings by hand per environment instead of using environment variables
Conflates package-level and project-level deployment models
Forgets that the master key password is required to move/restore the catalog across servers
Doesn't address how secrets (passwords) stay encrypted/marked Sensitive per environment

States the one-environment-per-execution rule explicitly
Describes a clean, repeatable promotion process across Dev/Test/Prod

questions.title: A Stored Procedure Is Recompiling Constantly Under Load
questions.prompt: A heavily-used stored procedure builds a large intermediate result set using a table variable, then joins it twice more inside the same procedure. Under load, you're seeing wildly inconsistent execution times and plan cache bloat. Diagnose why the table variable choice is likely the architectural root cause at this scale, and rewrite the approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Table variables historically carry no real statistics — on many compatibility levels the optimizer assumes roughly one row regardless of actual size — so when the intermediate set is genuinely large, the optimizer builds a plan sized for one row: an undersized memory grant and a join strategy that's wrong for the real row count. The inconsistent timing comes from actual row counts varying run to run while the cached plan was compiled against that wrong, fixed assumption, so some executions get lucky and others spill to disk or pick a bad join type. A #temp table, by contrast, gets real statistics maintained by SQL Server, letting the optimizer size the plan for the two downstream joins accurately. The tradeoff: a significant change in a temp table's row count can trigger a recompile — but that's a feature here, not a bug, since it means the plan adapts to actual data instead of staying wrong. The fix is to replace the DECLARE @T TABLE with a CREATE TABLE #T, optionally indexed if the joins warrant it, keeping the rest of the procedure's logic unchanged.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening here is that the optimizer doesn't have real numbers to work with. A table variable, on most compatibility levels, gets treated as roughly one row no matter how big it actually gets, so the plan built for it is sized for the wrong workload — that's exactly why the timing is inconsistent: the actual row count varies, but the plan doesn't adapt. My fix is to swap it for a #temp table, because SQL Server maintains real statistics on those, so the two downstream joins get a plan that's actually shaped for the data. I'll be upfront that this trades one problem for a different, much smaller one — a temp table can trigger a recompile when its row count shifts significantly — but I'd rather have an occasional recompile that produces a correct plan than a stable plan that's confidently wrong every time.
questions.example:
-- Before: table variable, optimizer assumes ~1 row
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @ActiveOrders TABLE (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    INSERT INTO @ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM @ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO

-- After: temp table, real statistics, optionally indexed
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    CREATE TABLE #ActiveOrders (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    CREATE INDEX IX_ActiveOrders_CustomerID ON #ActiveOrders (CustomerID);

    INSERT INTO #ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM #ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO

Doesn't connect inconsistent timing to missing statistics on a large table variable
Recommends a CTE instead, missing that a CTE is re-evaluated/inlined and doesn't solve the cardinality problem either
Adds an index to the table variable via inline constraint without recognizing its limits
Ignores the recompile tradeoff when switching to a temp table

questions.title: Fix a Non-SARGable, Non-Covering Query Under Load
questions.prompt:
You're handed this production query that's doing a full clustered index scan on a 40-million-row table, confirmed via SET STATISTICS IO showing logical reads in the hundreds of thousands:

SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) = '06/15/2013'
   AND UPPER(Status) = 'SHIPPED';

Rewrite the query to be SARGable, and write the covering index you'd create to support it, explaining your column order choice.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two non-SARGable predicates here, and both need fixing. CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) wraps the date column in a function, forcing a scan even if an index exists; UPPER(Status) does the same to the status column. The date predicate should be rewritten as a half-open range against the raw column; the status predicate should compare against the literal in its natural case, relying on the column's collation to be case-insensitive rather than forcing a transformation on every row. For the covering index, the equality predicate (Status) should lead the key, since equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index — this lets SQL Server seek to the exact Status value, then scan only the OrderDate range within that narrower slice — and the remaining selected columns go into INCLUDE so the plan never needs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index.
questions.example:
-- SARGable rewrite
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE Status = 'Shipped'
  AND OrderDate >= '2013-06-15' AND OrderDate < '2013-06-16';

-- Covering index: equality column first, then the range column, then INCLUDE the rest
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_SalesOrderHeader_Status_OrderDate
ON Sales.SalesOrderHeader (Status, OrderDate)
INCLUDE (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalDue);
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out there are actually two separate problems stacked in that one WHERE clause, not one. The CONVERT around OrderDate and the UPPER around Status are both doing the same damage — wrapping the column so the index can't be used no matter how well it's built. I'd rewrite the date as a range against the raw column and drop the UPPER, trusting the collation to handle case. Then for the index, I always put the equality column first — Status — because that lets SQL Server narrow down to an exact value before it even has to think about the date range, and I'd include the rest of the selected columns so we get a fully covering seek with no extra trip back to the clustered index.
commonMistakes: Only fixes one of the two non-SARGable predicates
Puts the range column before the equality column in the index key
Forgets INCLUDE columns, leaving a Key Lookup in the plan
Assumes UPPER() is needed without checking the column's collation
keyPoints: Identifies both non-SARGable predicates
Rewrites the date predicate as a range
Removes the function wrapper on Status, citing collation
Designs index key order correctly: equality before range
Makes the index covering with INCLUDE

questions.title: Write the SSIS Expression for a Parameterized Watermark Extract
questions.prompt: You're building the OLE DB Source for an incremental load. Write the SSIS Expression (for use in an Expression Task or a variable's EvaluateAsExpression property, not a straight SQL parameter) that builds a dynamic SQL command string filtering AdventureWorks2012's Sales.SalesOrderHeader to rows modified after a DateTime package variable @[User::LastLoadDate], correctly formatted for T-SQL. Also state where you'd actually set this up as an alternative to inline SQL parameters.
questions.modelAnswer: The SSIS Expression Language has no locale-safe, direct cast from a DateTime variable straight into a T-SQL date literal, so the standard pattern is to build the string manually: extract YEAR/MONTH/DAY (and, if time precision matters, hour/minute/second) from the variable with (DT_WSTR, n) casts, zero-pad the month/day/time components with RIGHT('0' + value, 2), and concatenate everything into an unambiguous 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MI:SS' literal assigned to a String variable, which an Execute SQL Task or a direct-input OLE DB Source then uses as its SQL command text. That said, the more robust, and actually preferred, approach — and the one this course's capstone uses — is to parameterize the OLE DB Source's SQL command with a '?' placeholder and map it to the LastLoadDate variable via the component's Parameter Mapping page, instead of hand-building a SQL string. Parameter mapping avoids both the date-formatting fragility and any injection-style risk, and should be the default; hand-built expression strings are reserved for cases a parameter placeholder genuinely can't cover, like constructing a dynamic table or file name.
questions.example:
"SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, soh.OrderDate, soh.ModifiedDate, sod.ProductID, sod.OrderQty, sod.UnitPrice, sod.LineTotal "
+ "FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader AS soh "
+ "JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID "
+ "WHERE soh.ModifiedDate > '"
+ (DT_WSTR,4)  YEAR( @[User::LastLoadDate] ) + "-"
+ RIGHT("0" + (DT_WSTR,2) MONTH( @[User::LastLoadDate] ), 2) + "-"
+ RIGHT("0" + (DT_WSTR,2) DAY( @[User::LastLoadDate] ), 2) + " "
+ RIGHT("0" + (DT_WSTR,2) DATEPART("hh", @[User::LastLoadDate] ), 2) + ":"
+ RIGHT("0" + (DT_WSTR,2) DATEPART("mi", @[User::LastLoadDate] ), 2) + ":"
+ RIGHT("0" + (DT_WSTR,2) DATEPART("ss", @[User::LastLoadDate] ), 2)
+ "'"
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, my first instinct whenever I see someone reaching for this kind of hand-built expression is to ask whether they actually need to. The expression language doesn't have a clean, locale-safe way to turn a DateTime into a SQL literal, so if I do have to build it, I'm zero-padding every component by hand — month, day, hour, minute, second — because '2024-6-5' is a string SQL Server might parse differently depending on settings, and that's exactly the kind of bug that only shows up weeks later. But I'd tell the interviewer straight: in practice I almost always skip this entirely and use Parameter Mapping with a '?' placeholder instead, because it sidesteps the formatting risk and the injection-style risk at the same time. I only reach for the string-building approach when a parameter placeholder genuinely isn't available, like building a dynamic file name.

Builds the SQL string but overlooks that this reintroduces the same injection-style risk a '?' parameter avoids
Doesn't know the simpler parameter-mapping alternative exists and over-engineers string building everywhere
Confuses the SSIS Expression Language with T-SQL syntax (e.g. using GETDATE() instead of the expression language's functions)

questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker — the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream — and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id — that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long — a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly — because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions — it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone — that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
commonMistakes: Immediately KILLs a session without identifying the actual head blocker first
Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain — not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting
Treats sp_who2 output alone as sufficient without the actual SQL text or wait info
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the head-blocker query pattern using DMVs
Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
Describes a safe escalation path (investigate before KILL)
Connects the fix back to root cause (missing index, long transaction, app behavior)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working query identifying the head blocker
Explains the DMV logic clearly
Describes a safe, sensible escalation/response procedure
Connects to durable root-cause fix, not just killing sessions

questions.title: Script a Dev/Test/Prod Environment Setup for a Deployed Project
questions.prompt: Rather than clicking through SSMS dialogs, write the T-SQL using SSISDB catalog stored procedures to: create a folder, create a 'Production' environment inside it, add a sensitive environment variable for a connection password, and reference that environment from an already-deployed project. Explain why you'd script this instead of doing it by hand in a real client engagement.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd use catalog.create_folder to create the folder, catalog.create_environment to create the Production environment inside it, catalog.create_environment_variable with the sensitive flag set to 1 for the password so SSISDB encrypts it under the catalog's master key, and catalog.create_environment_reference to actually link that environment to the already-deployed project — this last step is easy to forget, and without it the project has no way to resolve parameters from the environment at execution time. I'd script this rather than click through SSMS because it's repeatable and idempotent across Dev, Test, and Production — the exact same script, with different values, removes the manual-dialog drift that's a common real cause of 'it works in Test but not in Prod.' It also means the environment setup can be checked into source control alongside the project and run as part of a release pipeline, so the whole promotion is auditable and can be re-run from scratch if an environment is ever rebuilt.
questions.professionalAnswer: On a real engagement I won't click through the SSMS dialogs for this, and I'd explain why: I want the exact same script to create Dev, Test, and Production, just with different values plugged in, because that's what actually guarantees there's no drift between environments. I'd script create_folder, then create_environment, then create_environment_variable — making sure the sensitive flag is set on anything like a password so it's encrypted under the catalog's master key — and then, critically, create_environment_reference, because I've seen people stop right before that step and wonder why the project still isn't picking up the environment. I'd also point out that this script belongs in source control next to the project itself, not just run once and forgotten.
commonMistakes: Forgets to mark the password variable as sensitive
Scripts the environment but never actually creates the environment_reference, leaving the project unable to resolve it
Assumes this is purely cosmetic rather than a real repeatability/auditability win
Hardcodes the secret value in a script that then gets checked into source control unencrypted
keyPoints: Uses the correct catalog stored procedures in the right order
Correctly marks secrets as sensitive
Creates the environment reference, not just the environment
Explains the repeatability/source-control argument for scripting over manual dialogs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working catalog stored procedure calls in the right sequence
Secrets correctly marked sensitive
Environment reference correctly created, linking project to environment
Explains the engagement-level rationale for scripting this

questions.title: Replace a Row-by-Row Price Update With a Set-Based Rewrite
questions.prompt: A nightly job uses a cursor to apply a different percentage increase to ListPrice per product category, reading category-specific rates from a rates table. It takes 40 minutes against 2 million products. Rewrite it as a single set-based statement.
questions.modelAnswer: The cursor's cost comes from processing one row at a time — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, each with its own overhead, multiplied by two million. SQL Server's storage engine is built to process sets of rows efficiently, so the fix is to express the same logic as a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, letting the engine apply the whole operation at once instead of looping. I'd use ISNULL to handle any product whose subcategory has no matching rate, so it's left unchanged rather than silently zeroed out by a NULL multiplication. I'd check that the join column is indexed before declaring victory, and only consider batching the update (e.g., with TOP(n) in a loop) if the single statement itself causes problematic lock duration or transaction log growth at this volume — I wouldn't reach for batching as the first move.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty minutes for two million rows is a huge tell that something's being processed one row at a time, and sure enough, that's exactly what the cursor is doing — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, over and over. My rewrite is a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, because that lets the storage engine do what it's actually built for, which is operating on a whole set at once instead of looping. The one detail I wouldn't skip is handling products whose subcategory has no matching rate — I use a LEFT JOIN with ISNULL so those rows just stay unchanged instead of silently getting multiplied by a NULL. And I'd check the join column has an index before I call this done, because a 40-minute cursor sometimes hides a missing index underneath it too.
commonMistakes: Keeps per-row logic inside a WHILE loop over a temp table, which is just a hand-rolled cursor
Forgets to handle categories with no matching rate row (NULL rate silently zeroing the increase)
Doesn't check whether the join column is indexed before declaring victory
Jumps to batching/chunking as the first solution instead of trying the plain set-based statement first
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the cursor as the core bottleneck, not server hardware
Produces a correct, equivalent set-based UPDATE...FROM
Handles the no-matching-rate case correctly (ISNULL or join behavior)
Considers indexing and batching only as secondary, scale-driven refinements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses cursor overhead as root cause
Produces a correct, working set-based rewrite
Handles edge cases (no matching rate) correctly
Discusses sensible secondary considerations (indexing, batching) without over-engineering

questions.title: The Nightly ETL Window Keeps Growing and Will Blow Its SLA
questions.prompt: You're the architect on a client engagement. Their nightly SSIS ETL load currently finishes in 3.5 hours inside a 4-hour window, but it's grown by roughly 15 minutes a month for the last six months as source data volume grows, and will blow the SLA within about 3 months on the current trend. Walk through your root-cause diagnosis process AND the long-term architectural fix you'd propose, including tradeoffs.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd determine whether the growth is linear with data volume — expected and structural — or disproportionate, which would point to something actively degrading, like index fragmentation, stale statistics, or a full-reload pattern whose cost scales with the entire table rather than the daily change. I'd check whether the heaviest packages are doing a full truncate-and-reload rather than an incremental, watermark-based load, and I'd pull the Integration Services Dashboard and Execution Performance reports — which require logging level Performance or Verbose to show per-component detail — to find exactly which data flow is actually growing fastest, rather than guessing. The long-term fix is to convert the heaviest full-load packages to incremental, watermark-based loads, which changes the growth curve from scaling with total source size to scaling with daily change volume — normally far flatter over time. Where a genuine full refresh is unavoidable, I'd consider partition switching for fact tables (bulk-load into a staging partition, then switch it in), disabling and rebuilding nonclustered indexes around a large load rather than maintaining them row by row, and parallelizing independent child packages via the master/child pattern instead of running them sequentially. The tradeoffs are real: incremental loads add watermark-management complexity and a new failure mode (missed or duplicate windows) that has to be handled idempotently; partition switching requires the fact table to already be partitioned and adds DDL complexity; and index rebuild windows need their own scheduling discipline so they don't themselves start threatening the SLA.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the client this isn't a 'speed up one query' problem — it's a growth-curve problem, and I want to treat it that way from the start. My first move is to separate expected growth from something actively degrading, which means pulling the actual execution history, not guessing. If the heaviest packages are still doing full truncate-and-reload every night, that's usually the headline finding, because that pattern's cost scales with the whole table, not with what actually changed. My recommendation is almost always to convert those to incremental, watermark-based loads first, because that one change bends the growth curve from 'scales with total data' to 'scales with daily change' — which is a completely different trajectory. Where a full refresh really can't be avoided, I'll bring in partition switching and smarter index maintenance, and I'll look at whether independent loads are needlessly running one after another instead of in parallel. I'm always honest that none of this is free — incremental loads mean I now have to get idempotency right, and partitioning adds real schema complexity — but I'd rather make that tradeoff deliberately now than watch the SLA breach happen on autopilot in three months.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a tuning problem (speed up one query) instead of an architecture/growth-curve problem
Proposes 'just run it in a bigger window' without addressing the trend
Doesn't check whether packages are full-load vs incremental before proposing fixes
Parallelizes independent child packages without first confirming they're actually independent
Never measures per-component cost before proposing where to optimize
keyPoints: Separates linear/expected growth from disproportionate/degrading growth
Uses real execution data (Dashboard/Execution Performance) rather than guessing
Identifies full-load-vs-incremental as the primary lever at this point
Considers partition switching and index rebuild strategy for genuinely full loads
Proposes parallelizing independent child packages
Names the real tradeoffs of each fix, not just the upside

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Presents a structured, evidence-based root-cause diagnosis
Proposes a durable architectural fix (not just 'optimize one query')
Covers incremental loads, partitioning, parallelism as concrete levers
Honestly states tradeoffs of the proposed fix

questions.title: A Junior Dev's Incremental Load Silently Double-Counts Rows
questions.prompt: A junior developer built an incremental-load package using the watermark pattern: read last load's max ModifiedDate, extract rows newer than it, load them, then update the watermark. After a mid-run failure and restart, finance reports the fact table has duplicate rows for the same order. Diagnose exactly what went wrong and redesign the load so it's idempotent and safely restartable.
questions.modelAnswer: The likely cause is that the package extracted and inserted a batch of rows, then failed before the final 'update watermark' task ran — perhaps the data flow itself failed partway, or the watermark-update step failed or was skipped. On restart, the watermark is still the old value, so the package re-extracts and re-inserts rows it already successfully loaded on the previous run; a plain INSERT duplicates them. The real design flaw is treating 'extract, load, then update watermark' as if it were one atomic unit, when a sequence of separate tasks isn't atomic across a failure. The fix has three parts. First, make the load itself idempotent regardless of whether it's a first or repeated attempt: replace a blind INSERT with a MERGE (or a Lookup-plus-Conditional-Split insert/update pattern) keyed on the business key, so reprocessing the same extracted rows updates existing rows instead of duplicating them. Second, make the watermark update strictly the last step, gated by the success of the data flow via a precedence constraint, so a failure before it can't leave a half-applied state the caller mistakes for complete — with the idempotent MERGE as the safety net for any gap that boundary doesn't fully cover. Third, add a checkpoint at the control-flow level so a failure restarts at the correct task instead of from the beginning, shrinking the window where this matters at all. It's also worth distinguishing restartability (resuming where you left off) from idempotency (safe to reprocess the same data twice) explicitly — this bug is really an idempotency gap, not a restartability one.
questions.example:
-- Idempotent load: MERGE instead of blind INSERT, keyed on the business key
MERGE INTO dbo.FactOrderSales AS tgt
USING stg.ExtractedOrders AS src
    ON tgt.SalesOrderID = src.SalesOrderID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET tgt.OrderQty = src.OrderQty, tgt.ExtendedAmount = src.ExtendedAmount
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (SalesOrderID, DateKey, ProductKey, OrderQty, ExtendedAmount)
    VALUES (src.SalesOrderID, src.DateKey, src.ProductKey, src.OrderQty, src.ExtendedAmount);

-- The watermark update now only ever runs after the MERGE succeeds, as the last task,
-- so even a repeated run with a stale watermark is harmless (upsert, not insert)
questions.professionalAnswer: What actually happened here is a timing gap, not a logic bug in the watermark itself. The package extracted and inserted a batch, then died before it got to update the watermark, so the next run still thinks it needs to pull those same rows — and because the load was a blind INSERT, it just duplicates them. I'd explain to the team that the real fix isn't 'add more error handling around the same design,' it's making the load itself safe to run twice: swap the INSERT for a MERGE keyed on the business key, so reprocessing the same rows updates them instead of duplicating them. I'd also make sure the watermark update is strictly the last thing that happens, gated on the data flow actually succeeding. And I'd be explicit with the junior dev about the distinction between restartability — picking up where you left off — and idempotency — being safe to run the same thing twice. This bug is really an idempotency gap wearing a watermark costume.
commonMistakes: Diagnoses it as 'the watermark logic is buggy' without identifying the actual non-atomic failure window
Fixes it by just adding more error handling around the same blind-INSERT design
Assumes a database transaction alone solves it, without addressing that the extract and the external watermark state can still diverge
Doesn't distinguish restartability (resuming where you left off) from idempotency (safe to reprocess the same data twice)
Proposes deleting and reloading everything as the 'fix', reintroducing the full-reload problem this pattern was built to avoid
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the non-atomic extract/load/watermark-update sequence as the root cause
Distinguishes idempotency from restartability explicitly
Redesigns the load itself (MERGE/upsert) to be safe under reprocessing
Ties the watermark update's timing/ordering to the load's actual success
Considers checkpoints and batch auditing as complementary, not substitute, fixes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the non-atomic failure window as root cause
Redesigns the load to be idempotent (MERGE/upsert) with correct example
Explicitly distinguishes idempotency from restartability
Proposes complementary safeguards (checkpoints, batch auditing)

questions.title: Package Runs Clean in SSDT, Fails Every Time From the Agent Job
questions.prompt: A newly deployed package runs perfectly when a developer executes it inside SSDT, but fails immediately every time SQL Server Agent runs it on schedule. Walk through your diagnosis, in order, and the fix you'd standardize so this stops recurring across the whole project.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start from the actual evidence, not a guess: pull the Agent job step's history output and the SSISDB catalog's Execution Performance / All Messages report for the real error text. The single most common root cause at this point is an identity mismatch — SSDT runs under the developer's own Windows login with their mapped drives and permissions, while the Agent job step runs under whatever account is configured on 'Run as,' typically the SQL Server Agent service account by default, which usually lacks access to the same file shares, database logins, or credential stores. A second thing I'd check is whether the job step's Configuration tab references the correct Environment — a job pointed at the wrong environment reference can resolve parameters to the wrong (e.g., Dev) values in a Production run, which produces a failure that can look superficially similar. Occasionally it's a 32-bit versus 64-bit provider mismatch if the error names a missing driver. The standardized fix, not a one-off patch: set up a dedicated proxy account with exactly the access the packages actually need — never the raw Agent service account, never a developer's personal login — and require every job step across the project to use that proxy and an explicit environment reference, so this class of failure doesn't need re-diagnosing package by package going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of the most common calls I get, and I never start by assuming the package logic is wrong, because it already proved itself in SSDT. The first thing I pull is the actual error text from the job history or the catalog's execution reports — I'm not going to theorize from 'it just fails.' Nine times out of ten it comes down to identity: SSDT ran as the developer, with their permissions and their mapped drives, and the Agent job is running as something else entirely, usually the Agent service account, which doesn't have the same access. I'd also double check the job step is pointed at the right environment reference, because a wrong environment can produce a failure that looks similar but is actually a config mismatch, not a permissions one. My fix isn't just to patch this one job — it's to set up a proper proxy account with exactly the access these packages need and require every job step on the project to use it, so we're not having this same conversation next month about a different package.
commonMistakes: Assumes the package itself is broken and starts debugging data flow logic instead of checking identity/permissions first
Doesn't pull the actual error text from the job/catalog reports before theorizing
Fixes this one job by hand instead of standardizing a proxy-account pattern for the whole project
Overlooks that a wrong environment reference can masquerade as this same kind of failure
keyPoints: Orders diagnosis correctly: get real error text before theorizing
Identifies account/permission mismatch as the most common root cause
Checks environment reference misconfiguration as a secondary cause
Proposes a standardized proxy-account fix at the project level, not a one-off patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, ordered diagnostic sequence starting from actual error evidence
Identifies the account/permission mismatch as the primary cause
Identifies environment-reference misconfiguration as a secondary cause
Proposes a standardized, project-wide fix rather than a one-off patch

questions.title: Nightly Load and Morning Reports Are Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: The nightly ETL load now runs long enough to overlap with early-morning reporting queries, and you're seeing a spike in deadlock errors (1205) exactly in that overlap window. Write the query you'd use to capture the actual deadlock graphs (not just the error count), and describe the architectural fix once you've confirmed the access pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server Profiler is deprecated, so I'd capture real deadlock graphs through Extended Events — either reading the always-on system_health session's xml_deadlock_report, or standing up a dedicated session — and extract the XML to see exactly which two statements and which objects/lock modes were involved. That turns 'we have deadlocks' into a concrete finding, like 'the ETL's bulk insert into FactOrderSales and a reporting SELECT doing a range scan are colliding on the same rows.' Once that's confirmed, I'd rank the fix options by durability: first, enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so reporting SELECTs stop taking the shared locks that participate in the deadlock at all, which addresses it structurally rather than by luck of timing; second, shrink and restructure the ETL's transactions so they hold locks for the shortest possible time and touch narrower row ranges, through smaller batches or partition-aligned loads; third, if this keeps recurring, separate the workloads architecturally — widen or shift the load window, or move reporting onto a readable secondary — so the two workloads stop contending for the same locks on the same instance entirely. I'd recommend RCSI as the fast structural win and workload separation as the long-term answer if the overlap keeps growing.
questions.example:
-- Query system_health's ring buffer for recent deadlock graphs
SELECT
    xed.value('(event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS EventTime,
    xed.query('.') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file('system_health*.xel', NULL, NULL, NULL) AS f
CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(f.event_data AS XML) AS xed) AS d
WHERE xed.value('(event/@name)[1]', 'varchar(100)') = 'xml_deadlock_report'
ORDER BY EventTime DESC;
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't propose a fix off an error count alone — I want the actual deadlock graph first, so I'm pulling it from the system_health Extended Events session rather than reaching for Profiler, which is deprecated at this point. Once I can see exactly which two statements and which rows are colliding, I can say something specific, like 'the nightly bulk insert and a reporting range scan are fighting over the same rows,' instead of just 'we have deadlocks.' From there, my go-to structural fix is read-committed snapshot isolation, because it takes the reporting side out of the locking picture entirely instead of just making it less likely to collide. If the client's really pushing both workloads hard, I'd also talk about shrinking the ETL's transactions and, longer term, moving reporting to a readable secondary — but I'd never reach for NOLOCK as the answer here, because trading a deadlock for a dirty read isn't actually a fix.
commonMistakes: Tries to diagnose deadlocks from just the error count/frequency instead of capturing the actual graph
Jumps straight to NOLOCK on the reporting queries as a 'fix', reintroducing dirty-read risk
Only addresses the symptom (overlap timing) without checking whether RCSI would remove the lock conflict structurally
Recommends a replica without first confirming the deadlock is lock-contention, not resource-contention
keyPoints: Uses Extended Events (not deprecated Profiler) to capture real deadlock graphs
Translates the captured graph into a concrete statement-level root cause before proposing a fix
Evaluates RCSI as a structural fix for reader/writer lock conflicts
Considers transaction shrinkage and workload separation (replica) as complementary long-term fixes
Avoids NOLOCK as a quick-fix answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct approach to capturing real deadlock graph evidence
Correctly reasons from captured evidence to root cause
Proposes RCSI or equivalent structural fix with justification
Considers workload separation/transaction design as durable long-term fix

questions.title: Design a Highly Available SSIS Deployment Across Two Data Centers
questions.prompt: A client wants their nightly SSIS-driven warehouse load to survive a complete data-center outage with minimal manual intervention. Design a highly-available SSIS deployment across two data centers with automated failover, covering the SSIS Catalog itself, package execution, and scheduling — and call out what this design does NOT solve.
questions.modelAnswer: The key insight is that SSIS itself has no native clustering or HA — its catalog, SSISDB, is just an ordinary SQL Server database, so HA for SSIS really means HA for the SQL Server instance(s) hosting SSISDB, plus a scheduling layer that can actually trigger executions from either side. I'd host SSISDB in an Always On Availability Group spanning both data centers — synchronous commit to a local-DC replica for zero data loss, asynchronous to the DR site if cross-site latency is too high for synchronous commit — so the catalog's projects, packages, parameters, and execution history fail over as part of the AG. I'd create matching Environments per data center within each folder, so DC-specific connection strings and file paths resolve correctly no matter which side is currently primary. SQL Server Agent jobs need to be mirrored on both instances, with the DR side's jobs disabled by default and enabled only by the same failover automation or runbook that promotes the AG — a failover that moves the data but doesn't start triggering jobs on the new primary isn't actually highly available. The source and destination databases the packages depend on need to sit within the same failover boundary as SSISDB, since a package that's 'HA' but reads from a source database that didn't fail over is still broken. And I'd script the catalog deployment via stored procedures so both sides stay in exact version lockstep, since failing over to a stale DR catalog is its own outage. What this design explicitly does not solve: an in-flight package execution at the moment of failover is lost and must restart, not resume mid-flight, so idempotent, watermark-based, checkpointed packages are a prerequisite for 'minimal manual intervention' to actually be true — and it says nothing about upstream source-system availability, which is a separate DR conversation entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd want the client to understand up front is that SSIS doesn't have HA of its own — the catalog is just a SQL Server database, so getting this right means getting SQL Server HA right, then layering scheduling on top. I'd put SSISDB in an Always On Availability Group across both data centers, synchronous locally and asynchronous to the DR site, so the whole catalog — packages, parameters, history — moves with a failover. But I'd stop them if they thought that was the whole answer, because the catalog failing over doesn't mean anything actually runs afterward — the Agent jobs on the DR side need to be part of the same failover automation, or you've got a perfectly replicated catalog that nobody's triggering. I'd also make sure the source and destination databases are in that same AG boundary, because an HA ETL layer reading from a non-HA source database is a false sense of security. And I'd be upfront about the one thing this doesn't solve: whatever was mid-execution at the moment of failover is gone, not resumed, so this design only delivers 'minimal manual intervention' if the packages themselves are already idempotent and checkpointed.
commonMistakes: Treats SSIS as something that has its own native clustering/HA, rather than building HA around SSISDB as an ordinary SQL Server database
Forgets to make Agent jobs failover-aware, so the catalog moves but nothing schedules executions on the new primary
Doesn't scope environments per data center, so failover runs with the wrong connection strings
Ignores that source/destination databases also need to be in the same HA boundary
Presents the design as solving in-flight execution loss without requiring idempotent/checkpointed packages first
keyPoints: Correctly frames HA for SSIS as HA for SQL Server hosting SSISDB (Always On AG)
Addresses environment scoping per data center
Addresses Agent job failover, not just data failover
Covers source/destination database HA boundary alignment
Explicitly states what the design does not solve (in-flight execution loss) and the prerequisite (idempotent/checkpointed packages)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SSISDB/Always On AG as the HA foundation
Addresses environment and job scheduling failover, not just data
Addresses source/destination database HA alignment
Honestly states the design's limitations and prerequisites

questions.title: Design a Multi-Environment Promotion Pipeline With Security Hardening
questions.prompt: Design the end-to-end promotion pipeline for a growing SSIS codebase: multiple developers, a master/child package architecture, and a requirement that no one without explicit sign-off can touch Production. Cover source control, the master/child structure, catalog folder/permission structure, and how a change actually reaches Production.
questions.modelAnswer: Source control holds the project files, with .ispac build artifacts produced by an automated build step (MSBuild or a CI pipeline), never hand-built on a developer's own machine for anything beyond quick Dev testing. I'd decompose the warehouse load into single-responsibility child packages — one per dimension or fact area — called by a master orchestrator via Execute Package Task, so a change to one dimension's load doesn't require retesting the entire refresh, and independent children can run in parallel to help the SLA. For the catalog, I'd use separate SSISDB folders per environment (or fully separate instances for Production on larger engagements), with folder-level permissions via MANAGE_OBJECT_PERMISSIONS granted only to the roles that need them: developers get rights on Dev/Test folders only, and a dedicated release/ops role, or the service account behind the CI/CD pipeline, is the only identity with deploy rights on the Production folder. Each folder gets its own Environment, consistent with the one-environment-per-execution rule. The promotion flow: a developer's change merges to a release branch, CI builds the versioned .ispac, it auto-deploys to Test's folder and runs an automated smoke test, and a sign-off gate — a named approver in the CI/CD tool, or a documented manual approval — is required before that exact same build artifact, never a rebuild, is deployed to Production. Promoting the identical tested artifact matters specifically to avoid 'it was different by the time it reached Prod.' Scheduling in Production is owned by the ops role, with Agent jobs referencing the Production environment and running under least-privilege proxy accounts, not the Agent service account and not a developer's login.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this so that reaching Production is never a matter of someone remembering to be careful — it has to be structurally impossible to skip the gate. Everything starts in source control, and the only .ispac that's ever built is the one CI produces, never something assembled by hand on a laptop. I'd push hard on decomposing the warehouse load into master/child packages too, because that's what makes it realistic to test one dimension's change without re-validating the whole load every time. On the catalog side, Production gets its own folder with permissions locked down to a release role or the CI service account — developers simply don't have rights there, full stop. The promotion itself goes build once in CI, auto-deploy to Test, run a smoke test, then require a named sign-off before that exact same artifact — not a rebuild — gets deployed to Production. And scheduling in Production runs under a dedicated, least-privilege proxy account, never the Agent service account and never someone's personal login.
commonMistakes: Lets developers deploy their own packages directly to Production 'just this once'
Rebuilds the .ispac for Production instead of promoting the exact tested artifact
Grants Production folder permissions broadly instead of to a dedicated release role/service account
Skips automated smoke testing in Test before the sign-off gate
Ignores that master/child decomposition is itself a prerequisite for safe, independently-testable promotion
keyPoints: Describes source control and CI-built, versioned .ispac artifacts
Uses master/child decomposition for independent testability and parallelism

questions.title: Design a Star Schema With Type 2 History for a New Subject Area
questions.prompt: The client wants a new 'Employee Performance' subject area added to their existing warehouse, with full historical tracking of employee department/title changes over time, and fast year-over-year aggregate reporting. As the architect, design the star schema (fact + dimension DDL sketch) and explain how SCD Type 2 and surrogate keys fit together to make this correct.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design one fact table, FactEmployeePerformance, at the grain of one row per employee per review period, surrounded by DimEmployee, DimDate, and possibly DimDepartment if department attributes need independent tracking — otherwise I'd denormalize the department name directly onto DimEmployee to keep the star's one-join-away shape simple. DimEmployee needs full Type 2 tracking, since department and title changes are exactly what this requirement asks to historize: it carries a surrogate EmployeeKey as its clustered primary key, the natural EmployeeID as a business key, and StartDate/EndDate/IsCurrent columns. Every department or title change closes the current row (sets EndDate, IsCurrent = 0) and inserts a new row with a new surrogate key, a fresh StartDate, and IsCurrent = 1 — never an in-place UPDATE of the changing attribute. The critical design decision is that FactEmployeePerformance stores the surrogate EmployeeKey, not the natural EmployeeID, so every performance review row permanently points at the exact version of the employee's department/title that was true at review time; year-over-year reports then correctly reflect what was true then, not what's true now, which a Type 1 overwrite would silently corrupt. For indexing, DimEmployee clusters on the narrow, ever-increasing surrogate key, with a unique nonclustered index on (EmployeeID, StartDate) to support the ETL's 'which version was active on this date' lookup; the fact table gets nonclustered indexes on each dimension foreign key to support the one-join-away reporting pattern efficiently.
questions.professionalAnswer: The requirement that actually drives this whole design is 'full historical tracking of department and title changes,' so I know immediately this is a Type 2 dimension, not Type 1. I'd build FactEmployeePerformance at one-row-per-employee-per-review-period, with DimEmployee, DimDate, and department info either denormalized onto the employee dimension or split out only if it needs its own independent history. The detail I'd walk through carefully is that the fact table has to store the surrogate EmployeeKey, never the natural EmployeeID — because that surrogate is what pins a review to the exact version of the employee's department and title that was true at that moment. If we stored EmployeeID instead, a promotion six months from now would silently rewrite what last year's review 'said' about the employee's department, which is exactly the kind of quiet history corruption the client is asking us to avoid. I'd cluster the dimension on a narrow surrogate key for insert performance and add a unique index on the business key plus StartDate so the ETL can always find which version was active on a given date.
commonMistakes: Stores the natural EmployeeID in the fact table instead of the surrogate EmployeeKey, breaking Type 2 history
Uses Type 1 (overwrite) for an attribute the client explicitly wants historized
Normalizes the dimension the way an OLTP schema would, adding unnecessary joins to the star
Forgets the business-key-plus-effective-date index the ETL needs to find 'which version was active on this date'
Clusters the dimension on the natural key instead of a narrow surrogate
keyPoints: Correctly separates fact grain from dimension design
Uses a surrogate key in the fact table, not the natural key, to support Type 2 history
Implements StartDate/EndDate/IsCurrent Type 2 tracking correctly
Designs appropriate indexes for both the ETL lookup pattern and the reporting join pattern
Explains why Type 1 would be wrong for this specific requirement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct star schema design (fact grain, dimension structure)
