questions.title: Build an Idempotent Incremental Load With a Watermark Table and MERGE
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL incremental load pattern for loading new and changed rows from a Source.Orders table (with a reliable ModifiedDate column) into a warehouse staging table, using a persisted high-water-mark table rather than a hardcoded date. The load must be safe to re-run after a partial failure without producing duplicate or missed rows.
questions.modelAnswer: An incremental load built on a persisted watermark needs three properties to be truly safe to re-run: the watermark must only advance after the load of that batch is confirmed complete, not before; the extract window must use a half-open interval (>= last watermark AND < this batch's cutoff, captured once at the start of the run) so rows that arrive mid-run aren't silently skipped or double-counted; and the actual merge into staging must be set-based and re-runnable, meaning running it twice against the same source window produces the same end state, not duplicates. MERGE gives you that re-runnability for free because it matches on key and either updates or inserts, rather than blindly appending. The watermark update has to happen inside the same transaction as the load, or immediately after a verified-successful load, never before — if the watermark advances first and the load then fails, that batch's rows are silently never loaded again.
questions.example:
-- 1. Watermark table: one row per source/target pair, holding the last
--    successfully loaded point and nothing else.
CREATE TABLE etl.WatermarkControl (
    SourceName     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    LastWatermark  DATETIME2    NOT NULL
);

-- 2. Capture the batch window ONCE, before touching data, so a long-running
--    load can't shift its own goalposts mid-run.
DECLARE @BatchStart DATETIME2, @BatchEnd DATETIME2;

SELECT @BatchStart = LastWatermark
FROM etl.WatermarkControl
WHERE SourceName = 'Source.Orders';

SET @BatchEnd = SYSUTCDATETIME();  -- fixed cutoff for this run

-- 3. Pull the half-open window into staging. Re-running this extract with
--    the same @BatchStart/@BatchEnd is harmless -- it's a pure SELECT.
TRUNCATE TABLE stg.Orders_Batch;

INSERT INTO stg.Orders_Batch (OrderID, CustomerID, OrderTotal, ModifiedDate)
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderTotal, ModifiedDate
FROM Source.Orders
WHERE ModifiedDate >= @BatchStart
  AND ModifiedDate <  @BatchEnd;

-- 4. MERGE into the real staging/warehouse table. Re-running this MERGE
--    against the same batch is also harmless: existing OrderIDs get
--    updated in place, not duplicated.
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

MERGE stg.Orders AS tgt
USING stg.Orders_Batch AS src
    ON tgt.OrderID = src.OrderID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET tgt.CustomerID = src.CustomerID,
               tgt.OrderTotal = src.OrderTotal,
               tgt.ModifiedDate = src.ModifiedDate
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (OrderID, CustomerID, OrderTotal, ModifiedDate)
    VALUES (src.OrderID, src.CustomerID, src.OrderTotal, src.ModifiedDate);

-- 5. Only advance the watermark once the MERGE has actually committed its
--    rows -- in the SAME transaction, so a crash here rolls back both
--    together instead of leaving the watermark ahead of the data.
UPDATE etl.WatermarkControl
SET LastWatermark = @BatchEnd
WHERE SourceName = 'Source.Orders';

COMMIT TRANSACTION;
questions.professionalAnswer: The part people usually get wrong isn't the MERGE, it's the watermark bookkeeping around it. I always capture the batch window as two fixed values -- the last watermark and 'now' -- at the very start of the run, before I touch any data, so a load that takes ten minutes doesn't accidentally extend its own window partway through and either skip or double-count rows that land in that gap. Then the extract itself is just a plain SELECT against that fixed window, which is trivially safe to re-run because it has no side effects. The MERGE is what actually makes the load idempotent -- matching on the real key means running it twice against the same batch leaves the table in exactly the same state, not with duplicates. And the one rule I never break: the watermark only moves forward after the MERGE has committed, in the same transaction if at all possible. If I advance the watermark first and the load then fails, I've just told the system those rows were already loaded when they weren't, and nobody will ever notice until someone asks why a batch of orders went missing.
commonMistakes: Hardcodes a date instead of persisting and reading a real watermark
Captures the batch end time as SYSUTCDATETIME() freshly at extract time instead of a value fixed once, letting the window drift during a long run
Advances the watermark before confirming the load succeeded, risking silently skipped rows after a failure
Uses a plain INSERT instead of MERGE, producing duplicate rows on any re-run
Doesn't wrap the merge and watermark update in the same transaction
keyPoints: Uses a persisted watermark table, not a hardcoded date
Fixes the batch window (start and end) once at the start of the run, using a half-open interval
Uses MERGE so re-running the same batch is idempotent rather than duplicating rows
Advances the watermark only after the load is confirmed successful, ideally in the same transaction
Explains why this specific ordering is what makes the load safe to re-run after a partial failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct, idempotent T-SQL using a watermark table and MERGE
Correctly fixes the batch window once rather than letting it drift during the run
Advances the watermark only after a confirmed-successful load
Explains why this design survives a partial failure without duplicate or missed rows

questions.title: An SSIS Package Runs Fine in SSDT But Fails Only When Executed From the Catalog
questions.prompt: A package runs perfectly every time you execute it from SSDT on your own machine, but every execution from the SSISDB catalog on the server fails, with errors pointing at a connection manager and a flat file path. Walk through your diagnosis, covering the specific ways catalog execution differs from a design-time run.
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct to say 'it works on my machine' is actually the clue, because catalog execution differs from an SSDT run in several concrete ways that don't show up until you deploy. First, file paths: a flat file connection manager pointing at a path that exists on your laptop (or a mapped drive only you have) will fail the moment it runs under the service account on the server, which has no such drive and no such local folder -- the fix is a UNC path the service account actually has permission to reach, not a local or mapped-drive path. Second, environment-driven parameter values: in SSDT you're running with your project's default parameter values, but a catalog execution runs against whatever Environment is actually mapped to that execution -- if the environment reference is missing, misconfigured, or points at the wrong variable, the package can silently pick up a wrong or blank value for something like a connection string. Third, 32-bit vs 64-bit providers: SSDT's debugger defaults to running packages in 32-bit mode for design-time compatibility with some drivers, while the catalog runs packages through the 64-bit DTExec by default -- if a connection relies on a provider that's only installed in one bitness, the exact same package can succeed under one and fail under the other. Fourth, protection level and sensitive values: if the package's ProtectionLevel is EncryptSensitiveWithUserKey, sensitive values (like a password embedded in a connection string) are encrypted to your personal Windows profile and simply won't decrypt for the service account running it on the server -- the deployment needs EncryptSensitiveWithUserKey changed to something catalog-appropriate, or better, sensitive values pulled from catalog environment variables instead of being stored in the package at all. Fifth, the service account's actual file-system and network permissions on the server are not the same as yours, so a permissions error that never surfaces under your own account can appear the moment the package runs as the catalog's execution account. I'd check the catalog execution report's exact error text first, since it almost always names which of these it is, rather than guessing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The phrase 'works on my machine, fails on the server' always means something environmental changed, not that the package logic is wrong, so I don't start by re-reading the data flow. I start with the execution report in the catalog, because the real error message almost always points straight at one of a short list of usual suspects. Is the flat file path a local or mapped drive that only exists on my machine, instead of a UNC path the service account can actually reach? Is there an Environment reference attached to this execution at all, and does it actually map to the right variables, because a missing or wrong environment mapping means the package is quietly running with the wrong parameter values, not the ones I tested with. Is this a 32-bit-only driver that happened to work under SSDT's debugger but has no 64-bit counterpart installed on the server, since the catalog runs 64-bit by default. And if the error smells like a decryption problem, I check the package's protection level, because EncryptSensitiveWithUserKey ties sensitive values to my own Windows account and will never decrypt under the service account running it on the server. I work through those in order of how specific the error message is, rather than guessing at all of them at once.
commonMistakes: Assumes the package logic itself must be wrong instead of considering environment differences
Doesn't check whether file paths are local/mapped-drive paths invalid under the service account
Overlooks that an Environment reference might be missing or misconfigured for this specific execution
Ignores the 32-bit vs 64-bit provider difference between SSDT debug runs and catalog DTExec execution
Doesn't consider that ProtectionLevel (EncryptSensitiveWithUserKey) ties sensitive values to the developer's own account
keyPoints: Identifies file-path/UNC-path differences between a developer machine and the service account on the server
Checks whether the correct Environment is actually referenced by this catalog execution
Names the 32-bit vs 64-bit provider difference between SSDT debug and catalog DTExec execution
Identifies ProtectionLevel/EncryptSensitiveWithUserKey as a real cause of catalog-only failures
Starts diagnosis from the actual catalog execution report rather than guessing blind

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies file-path and service-account permission differences
Correctly identifies Environment-mapping as a possible cause
Names the 32-bit/64-bit provider distinction between SSDT and catalog execution
Identifies ProtectionLevel/sensitive-value encryption as a cause
Describes a structured diagnosis starting from the catalog execution report

questions.title: Two Parallel Child Packages in a Master Orchestrator Start Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: You designed a master package with two child packages loading DimCustomer and DimProduct in parallel, since they looked independent. In production, the run intermittently fails with SQL Server deadlock errors (1205) between the two child packages. Diagnose why packages that load two completely different dimension tables could be deadlocking each other, and fix the design.
questions.modelAnswer: Loading different target tables doesn't guarantee the two child packages don't touch the same resources. The most likely cause is that both children share a staging or lookup resource that isn't obvious from the dimension names alone -- for example, both packages might run an Execute SQL Task at the start that does something like TRUNCATE/DELETE against a shared staging schema, update a shared batch-control or audit table, or read a shared lookup table that one of them also writes to. Even without a shared table, both children might be inserting into tables that share a common parent via foreign-key constraints, or taking out page/table locks (on a small staging table, SQL Server can escalate to table-level locks) that collide even though the final destination tables differ. The real fix starts with pulling the actual deadlock graph (the xml_deadlock_report Extended Event), not guessing, to see the two exact statements and resources involved. Once identified, the durable fix depends on what's shared: if it's a common staging or control table, give each child its own staging table/partition instead of sharing one, so there's genuinely nothing to contend over; if it's a shared lookup table being read by one and written by another, sequence that write to happen before both children start, rather than mid-run; and if it's lock escalation on a small shared table, add indexing or explicitly manage locking (ROWLOCK hints, shorter transactions) so a full-table lock is never needed. 'They load different dimensions' was never actually evidence of independence -- only an explicit check of every resource each child package touches, not just its destination table, proves that.
commonMistakes: Assumes different destination tables guarantee no resource contention
Doesn't check for a shared staging, lookup, or batch-control table both children touch
Fixes it by simply making the children run sequentially instead of finding and removing the actual shared resource
Never pulls the actual deadlock graph before proposing a fix
Overlooks lock escalation on a small shared table as a contention source
keyPoints: Recognizes that different destination tables don't prove the packages are resource-independent
Identifies shared staging/control/lookup tables as the likely real point of contention
Insists on pulling the actual deadlock graph before proposing a fix
Proposes removing the shared contention point (separate control rows/tables, resequencing) rather than just serializing the children
Treats 'looks independent' as something to verify, not assume, before parallelizing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that shared resources, not destination tables, cause the deadlock
Names plausible shared resources (staging, control, lookup tables, lock escalation)
Insists on evidence (deadlock graph) before proposing a fix
Proposes a fix that removes the contention rather than just serializing the children

questions.title: Data-Driven Subscriptions Stop Firing After a Routine Service Account Password Rotation
questions.prompt: Every data-driven subscription on your report server stopped delivering reports overnight. No code or report changed. IT rotated the service account password used by the report server as part of routine security policy the same night. Walk through exactly why that rotation broke subscriptions, why it happened silently instead of raising an obvious alarm, and how you'd prevent a repeat.
questions.modelAnswer: Data-driven subscriptions depend on the report server's unattended execution account and the SQL Server Agent jobs that the Report Server Scheduling and Delivery Processor creates to trigger them -- there's no interactive user present when a subscription fires at 6 AM, so the report server has to authenticate as a saved account to query the delivery-recipient dataset and, depending on configuration, to run the report itself. When that account's password is rotated in Active Directory but not updated everywhere the report server has it cached -- the unattended execution account setting in Report Server configuration, and/or the SQL Server Agent proxy credential the subscription jobs run under -- every subscription that depends on that account starts failing authentication the instant the old cached password stops working. It happens silently rather than loudly because the failure occurs deep inside a scheduled job with no one watching it in real time, and because the report server's own event log entries for this are easy to miss unless subscription failures are actively monitored -- a failed subscription produces a failure row in the ReportServer database's execution log and an entry in the Windows Application log, but nothing surfaces to a human unless something is specifically watching for it. Prevention has two layers: first, immediate -- update the unattended execution account and any SQL Agent proxy/credential objects as part of the same change ticket that rotates the account's password, not as an afterthought discovered after subscriptions fail; second, durable -- add active monitoring that specifically checks subscription execution success/failure (querying the ReportServer database's execution log, or alerting on SQL Agent job failure for the relevant job category) so a broken subscription surfaces within minutes, not when a business user notices a report never arrived. I'd also push for a documented dependency list -- every service account rotation gets checked against a list of systems that cache that account's credentials, so report server subscriptions are never an afterthought discovered the hard way again.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway here is 'nothing in our code changed, but a password did' -- that's almost always an authentication problem on a scheduled process, because scheduled jobs are exactly the thing that quietly keeps using an old cached credential until someone notices. Subscriptions run unattended, so the report server needs a saved account -- the unattended execution account, and often a SQL Agent proxy credential for the job that actually triggers the subscription -- and if that password gets rotated in AD without also updating it in Report Server's configuration and in the Agent proxy, every subscription relying on it starts failing authentication at the exact moment the rotation takes effect. It's silent because a subscription failure doesn't page anyone by default -- it just writes a failure row into the execution log and moves on, and the first human to notice is usually a business user asking where their 6 AM report is. So my fix is two things: first, make the account update part of the same rotation ticket, not a follow-up task someone remembers later; and second, put real monitoring on subscription success/failure so a broken subscription surfaces to us in minutes, not whenever someone complains.
commonMistakes: Assumes a code, report, or data change caused the failure instead of considering the credential rotation
Doesn't identify the unattended execution account and/or SQL Agent proxy credential as the dependency that broke
Doesn't explain why the failure was silent (no active monitoring on subscription execution)
Proposes only a reactive fix (update the password) without a durable prevention (dependency checklist, monitoring)
Doesn't connect the failure to the Scheduling and Delivery Processor / SQL Agent job mechanism underneath subscriptions
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the unattended execution account and/or Agent proxy credential as what broke
Explains why the failure is silent by default (no active monitoring on subscription execution)
Proposes updating credentials as part of the same rotation change, not an afterthought
Proposes durable monitoring on subscription success/failure
Recommends a documented dependency list for future account rotations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the credential dependency underlying data-driven subscriptions
Explains why the failure was silent rather than immediately obvious
Proposes a concrete immediate fix
Proposes a durable prevention (monitoring, dependency checklist) for future rotations

questions.title: Gateway Cluster Refreshes Succeed on One Node and Time Out on Another
questions.prompt: Your organization runs an on-premises data gateway cluster with three nodes for high availability. Scheduled refreshes against the same dataset intermittently time out, and you notice the failures correlate with which node happened to pick up the request. Diagnose the likely causes in a gateway cluster specifically (not a single-gateway setup), and describe the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A gateway cluster's whole value proposition is that any node can service any request, with the Power BI service load-balancing across whichever nodes are online -- which means the most common cause of node-specific failures is that the nodes aren't actually equivalent. The leading suspect is driver or component drift: if the three machines don't have identical versions of the data source drivers (an ODBC driver, an OLE DB provider, a specific connector version) a query that one node's driver handles fine can hang or error on another node with an older or mismatched driver version. Second: gateway cluster members need their recovery key and configuration kept in sync, and a node that was added later, patched separately, or restored from an older config can silently diverge from the others in ways that don't show up until it happens to pick up a request. Third: network path differences -- if the three gateway machines sit in different subnets, behind different firewall rules, or have different latency/routing to the actual data source, a node that can't reach the source as reliably will time out exactly as intermittently as this symptom describes, while the other two nodes succeed every time. Fourth: resource contention on one node specifically -- if the three machines aren't sized or loaded identically (one also running other workloads), that node can be the one that times out under load while the others handle the same request fine. The fix is to first identify which specific node correlates with the failures (gateway cluster logs identify which node serviced each request), then diagnose that node specifically against the other two: compare driver/component versions, compare network reachability to the source, and compare the node's resource utilization during the failure window. The durable fix is configuration parity enforced as policy -- identical driver versions, identical patch level, and ideally machines provisioned from the same image or a documented build checklist -- rather than treating each node as independently maintained.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that makes this a cluster-specific problem, not a generic gateway problem, is that it only fails on certain nodes -- which tells me the three machines aren't actually identical, even though the whole point of a cluster is that they're supposed to be interchangeable. My first move is to use the gateway logs to confirm exactly which node served each failed request, so I'm not guessing. Then I compare that node against the other two on the things that actually cause this symptom: are the data source drivers the exact same version everywhere, is there a network path or firewall difference that makes that specific machine slower or less reliable reaching the source, and is that machine running other workloads that are stealing resources the other two don't have to compete with. Once I know which of those it is, the immediate fix is usually straightforward -- patch the driver, fix the network rule, rebalance the load. But the fix I actually care about is the policy one: these three machines need to be provisioned identically and kept in lockstep, patch for patch, driver for driver, because 'it's a cluster' only holds up if every node genuinely behaves the same way, and right now it doesn't.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a generic gateway timeout problem without addressing why it's specific to certain nodes in a cluster
Doesn't check for driver/connector version drift across the cluster's member machines
Overlooks network path or firewall differences specific to one node
Doesn't use gateway logs to confirm which node served each failed request before diagnosing
Fixes the immediate symptom without proposing configuration-parity policy across cluster nodes
keyPoints: Recognizes that a gateway cluster's nodes must be configuration-equivalent, and failures suggest they aren't
Identifies driver/connector version drift as a leading cause
Considers network path/firewall differences specific to one node
Considers resource contention from unequal workloads across nodes
Proposes using gateway logs to confirm the failing node before diagnosing, and configuration-parity policy as the durable fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a node-equivalence problem specific to clustering
Identifies driver/version drift as a leading cause
Identifies network/resource differences as plausible causes
Proposes a structured diagnosis using gateway logs and a durable configuration-parity fix

questions.title: Disaster Recovery Runbook for the SSISDB Catalog: RPO/RTO and the Master Key Problem
questions.prompt: Design a disaster-recovery runbook specifically for the SSISDB catalog -- not the source databases, the catalog itself, which holds every deployed project, parameter, environment, and execution history for your ETL platform. Cover what has to be backed up beyond the database file itself, how you'd restore the catalog onto a new instance, and your target RPO/RTO.
questions.modelAnswer: SSISDB is a real database, so it's covered by the same backup regime as every other critical database -- regular full backups plus transaction log backups on an interval tight enough to meet the RPO, since the catalog's execution history, environment variables, and parameter values all change as ETL runs and gets redeployed. But a database backup alone isn't sufficient for a full recovery, which is the detail people miss: SSISDB encrypts sensitive values (connection strings, passwords stored in parameters) using the database master key, protected by the password set when the catalog was first created. Restoring the SSISDB database onto a different instance without also having that master key backup and its password means the restored catalog comes up with encrypted values it can no longer decrypt -- projects deploy and appear present, but execute with broken connection managers. So the actual runbook has three backed-up artifacts, not one: the SSISDB database backups (full + log), a backup of the database master key (BACKUP MASTER KEY, taken whenever the catalog is created or the key is regenerated), and the master key password itself stored in a secrets vault, not a shared document. Restore procedure onto a new instance: restore the SSISDB database backup, then restore the master key using the backed-up key file and password (OPEN MASTER KEY ... DECRYPTION BY PASSWORD, then re-encrypt by the service master key on the new instance), and verify a known project's parameters decrypt correctly before declaring the catalog usable -- not just that the database attached. RPO/RTO targets: I'd set RPO to match the organization's tolerance for re-running ETL history and losing recent deployments -- typically the same log-backup interval used for the warehouse itself, often 15-30 minutes for a platform this critical, since losing recent execution history is a minor data-recovery annoyance but losing a recent deployment or parameter change is a real operational problem. RTO depends on whether this is a cold-standby restore (hours, limited by backup restore time) or whether the catalog's SQL Server instance is itself covered by a broader HA strategy like Always On, in which case the catalog fails over with everything else in minutes rather than requiring a manual restore at all -- I'd push for the catalog to ride on the same HA mechanism as the rest of the platform rather than being treated as a standalone recovery case, since it's no less critical than the data it orchestrates.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part of this that catches people out is assuming SSISDB is 'just a database' for backup purposes, when it's actually a database plus a dependency most people forget: the master key. If you restore SSISDB onto a new instance without also having a backup of that master key and the password that protects it, every encrypted connection string and sensitive parameter in the catalog comes back as garbage the new instance can't decrypt -- projects look deployed, but nothing actually runs. So my runbook has three things in it, not one: full and log backups of SSISDB itself on the same cadence as our other critical databases, a backup of the master key taken whenever it's created or changed, and the master key password living in a secrets vault, never in a shared doc next to the runbook. Restoring is: bring the database back, restore the master key against it, and then actually verify -- open a known project's parameters and confirm they decrypt -- before I tell anyone the catalog is back, because 'the database attached successfully' isn't the same thing as 'the catalog actually works.' For RPO and RTO, I'd tie this platform to whatever HA story the rest of our SQL Server estate has -- if we're running Always On elsewhere, I want the catalog's instance on it too, because treating ETL orchestration as a second-class recovery case compared to the data it's moving doesn't make sense to me.
commonMistakes: Treats SSISDB as covered by a generic database backup without mentioning the master key dependency
Doesn't back up the master key or document its password securely
Restores the database and declares success without verifying sensitive values actually decrypt
Sets RPO/RTO targets without justifying them against what's actually at risk (recent deployments/parameter changes vs. execution history)
Treats the catalog as a standalone recovery case instead of considering it should ride the platform's broader HA strategy

questions.title: Architecture Review: A Report Server Scale-Out Deployment for 10,000 Daily Subscription Deliveries
questions.prompt: Your organization's single report server instance is becoming a bottleneck: report rendering is slow during business hours, and the nightly batch of roughly 10,000 scheduled subscriptions regularly runs past its window. Design a report server scale-out deployment to fix this, and explain specifically how subscription processing is coordinated so the same subscription doesn't fire twice across multiple report server instances.
questions.modelAnswer: A report server scale-out deployment separates the stateless rendering tier from the shared state, which is exactly what this problem needs: multiple report server instances, each installed on its own machine, all pointed at the same single ReportServer and ReportServerTempDB databases rather than each maintaining its own. Because the databases -- not any individual report server machine -- hold the actual report definitions, schedules, subscriptions, and cached/snapshot data, any of the scaled-out instances can serve any interactive rendering request, and a load balancer (hardware NLB or a software equivalent) in front of the instances distributes that interactive load evenly, directly addressing the business-hours rendering bottleneck. For the 10,000-subscription nightly batch, the key mechanism is that the Scheduling and Delivery Processor component, which executes subscriptions, runs on every scale-out instance, but they all coordinate through the shared ReportServerTempDB -- when a scheduled job fires, the processor on whichever instance picks it up claims that specific subscription's execution in the shared database, which prevents any other instance from also processing it; this is what makes scale-out safe for subscription processing rather than a source of duplicate sends. With more instances, more subscriptions execute in parallel across the scale-out deployment within the same nightly window, directly solving the SLA problem -- though I'd also check whether the actual bottleneck for the overnight batch is report server compute at all, or whether it's the underlying data source (the same warehouse query running 10,000 times), since scale-out only helps the report-server-side part of that equation. I'd size the number of instances based on the real split between interactive daytime concurrency and overnight subscription throughput, since those are genuinely different workloads competing for the same scaled-out pool, and consider whether a dedicated subset of instances for overnight processing (via a scale-out deployment that's workload-aware) makes sense if the two workloads' peaks start to interfere with each other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this to the board as two separate problems that happen to share one fix. Daytime rendering is slow because one machine is serving every interactive request; scale-out fixes that directly, because every instance points at the same shared ReportServer database, so any of them can render any report, and a load balancer spreads that work around instead of piling it on one box. The subscription backlog is the question people actually worry about with scale-out, because the obvious fear is 'what stops two instances from firing the same subscription twice.' The answer is that the scheduling and delivery processing coordinates through the shared ReportServerTempDB -- whichever instance picks up a given subscription claims it there, so the others know not to touch it. That's what makes it safe to just add more instances and get more subscriptions processed in parallel within the same overnight window, instead of everything funneling through one machine's capacity. The one thing I'd flag honestly to the board: if the real bottleneck turns out to be the warehouse query underneath those reports, not the report server itself, scale-out helps the rendering tier but won't fix a slow data source running 10,000 times a night -- so I'd want us to confirm which half of the problem we're actually solving before we commit budget to more report server hardware.
commonMistakes: Proposes scale-out without explaining how subscription processing avoids duplicate execution across instances
Doesn't identify the shared ReportServer/ReportServerTempDB databases as what makes any instance interchangeable
Assumes scale-out alone fixes the problem without checking whether the underlying data source query is the real bottleneck
Doesn't distinguish daytime interactive load from overnight subscription throughput as different workloads on the same pool
Proposes scale-out as a purely hardware decision without mentioning the load balancer tier
keyPoints: Correctly describes scale-out as multiple instances sharing one ReportServer/ReportServerTempDB database
Explains how subscription coordination through the shared database prevents duplicate execution
Proposes a load balancer for interactive rendering traffic
Checks whether the real nightly bottleneck is report server compute or the underlying data source
Considers daytime vs. overnight workload differences when sizing the deployment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a scale-out deployment on shared ReportServer databases
Correctly explains the coordination mechanism preventing duplicate subscription execution
Addresses both the interactive-rendering and subscription-throughput problems distinctly
Questions whether the underlying data source, not just the report server, is the real bottleneck

questions.title: Architecture Review: A Multi-Tenant Power BI Embedded Platform for 200 External Customers
questions.prompt: Your company is building a SaaS product that embeds Power BI reports for 200 external customers, with a hard requirement that one customer must never be able to see even a trace of another customer's data. Design the architecture: the app-owns-data model, capacity sizing, and specifically how you'd guarantee tenant isolation.
questions.modelAnswer: For an external-facing SaaS product, this is the app-owns-data embedding model, not user-owns-data: the application authenticates to the Power BI service using a dedicated service principal (or master user account, though service principal is the modern, recommended path), and every customer who opens the embedded report is really an anonymous end user as far as Power BI is concerned -- the application itself controls what they see, through the embed token the app generates for each session. Tenant isolation, the hard requirement here, has to be enforced at two layers, not one: first, row-level security on the semantic model, scoped per customer, so even if every customer's data lives in one shared semantic model (the efficient, common pattern at this scale), the RLS role filters every query to that customer's rows only, and the embed token generation call explicitly specifies which RLS role and identity to apply for that session -- getting this binding wrong, generating a token without the correct effective identity, is the single most dangerous failure mode in this architecture, because it would let a customer's session see unfiltered data. Second, I would not rely on RLS alone for a hard '200 customers, zero tolerance for crossover' requirement -- I'd add workspace-level separation for at least any customer whose contract or risk profile demands it, with the option of per-customer or per-tier workspaces rather than always sharing one semantic model, trading operational simplicity for a harder isolation boundary where the business actually needs one. Capacity sizing: at 200 external customers, this needs a Premium or Fabric (F-SKU) capacity rather than per-user licensing, since end customers don't hold Power BI licenses in the embedded model; sizing targets peak concurrent embedded sessions plus whatever refresh load the shared or per-tenant semantic models generate, and I'd load-test with simulated concurrent sessions before committing to a specific SKU rather than estimating from a seat count that doesn't actually apply here. I'd also insist on an audit trail specifically logging which RLS role/identity was applied to every embed token generated, so an isolation failure -- however unlikely -- would be immediately traceable rather than discovered by a customer complaint.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd be most careful to get right here isn't the capacity sizing, it's the embed token generation, because that's the one place a mistake actually leaks data between customers. This is the app-owns-data model -- our application, not the individual customer, authenticates to Power BI, and every customer session is really just an identity our app asserts when it generates that session's embed token. If every customer shares one semantic model for efficiency, which is the common pattern at this scale, the embed token has to carry the correct RLS role and customer identity every single time, with no exceptions and no fallback path that generates a token without it -- that's the one bug that would actually violate the hard requirement here. Given how much is riding on 'zero tolerance for crossover,' I wouldn't lean on RLS as the only control for every customer -- for higher-risk or larger customers I'd put them in their own workspace entirely, so there's a harder boundary than a filter that has to be applied correctly on every single token. On capacity, since these are external users with no Power BI licenses of their own, this has to run on a Premium or Fabric capacity sized for peak concurrent embedded sessions, and I wouldn't commit to a SKU without actually load-testing simulated concurrency first. And I'd want every embed token's RLS role and identity logged, so if anything ever did go wrong, we'd know immediately and exactly how, instead of finding out from a customer.
commonMistakes: Confuses app-owns-data embedding with user-owns-data licensing, assuming customers need Power BI accounts
Treats RLS alone as sufficient for a zero-tolerance isolation requirement without considering workspace-level separation for higher-risk tenants
Doesn't identify embed token generation (RLS role/identity binding) as the actual point of failure risk
Sizes capacity by a per-user seat count instead of peak concurrent embedded sessions
Doesn't propose auditing which RLS role/identity was applied per session
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the app-owns-data embedding model and service principal authentication
Identifies embed token generation (RLS role/identity binding) as the critical isolation control and failure risk
Proposes workspace-level separation as a harder boundary for tenants where RLS alone is too risky
Sizes Premium/Fabric capacity against peak concurrent embedded sessions, not seat counts
Proposes auditing of RLS role/identity per embed token for traceability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the app-owns-data embedding architecture
Identifies embed token/RLS binding as the critical tenant-isolation control
Proposes workspace-level separation as an additional isolation layer where warranted
Sizes capacity correctly for an external embedded scenario
Proposes auditability of per-session RLS/identity binding

questions.title: Architecture Review Board: Repartitioning a Fact Table That Just Crossed 2 Billion Rows
questions.prompt: Your largest fact table just crossed 2 billion rows, was never partitioned, and nightly loads, index maintenance, and ad hoc queries against recent data are all degrading. Design the partitioning strategy you'd present to the review board, including the partition key choice, how you'd implement a sliding-window maintenance process, and how you'd actually migrate an unpartitioned 2-billion-row table into this scheme without an unacceptable outage.
questions.modelAnswer: Partition key choice: for a fact table at this scale, the date key (typically the integer DateKey surrogate already on the table, not a datetime column) is almost always correct, because it aligns with how the table is actually queried (recent-date-range queries dominate) and how it's maintained (old data ages out in date order, new data arrives in date order) -- a partition function on anything else, like a high-cardinality business key, wouldn't give you either benefit. I'd design monthly partitions for a table this size, rather than daily (too many partitions to manage, metadata overhead) or yearly (partitions too large to switch efficiently), using a partition function with monthly boundaries and a partition scheme mapping each partition to its own filegroup, so that I/O for recent-partition-heavy queries isn't contending with older, rarely-touched partitions on the same physical storage. Sliding-window maintenance: each month, a new empty partition is created ahead of time (SPLIT) for the upcoming month, new data for the completed prior month is loaded into a staging table with the identical schema and indexes, validated, then SWITCHED into its place in the fact table -- a metadata-only operation taking milliseconds, not a row-by-row insert. At the other end, a partition old enough to fall outside the retention window is SWITCHED OUT to an archive table (or dropped), again as metadata-only. This is what makes both new-data loads and old-data archiving fast regardless of total table size, because neither operation touches the other partitions. Migration without an unacceptable outage: this is the hard part at 2 billion rows, and a straight 'rebuild the table partitioned' approach would lock or scan the whole table for far too long. I'd use an online, staged approach: create the new partitioned table (same schema, with the partition function/scheme and all indexes built partition-aligned) alongside the existing table; backfill it in batches, oldest data first, each batch sized to avoid excessive log growth or blocking, running during low-traffic windows; once the backfill catches up to near-current data, switch over new incoming writes to the new table (via a view swap or a brief final cutover window for the most recent, smallest increment of data); validate row counts and key aggregates match between old and new; then rename the new table into the old table's place and decommission the original. The only unavoidable 'outage,' if any, is the brief final cutover for the last small increment, not a wholesale rebuild of 2 billion rows under a lock.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open with the partition key, because that's the decision the rest of the design hangs off: it's the date key, almost certainly, because that's both how people query this table -- mostly recent date ranges -- and how we maintain it -- old data ages out, new data arrives, both in date order. I'd go monthly rather than daily or yearly, because daily is too many partitions to administer and yearly partitions are too big to switch efficiently. Once that's set, the maintenance story is what actually solves the nightly-load and index-maintenance pain: each month we stage the new month's data into a table shaped exactly like one partition, validate it, and SWITCH it in -- that's a metadata operation, not a 2-billion-row insert, and the same thing in reverse ages old data out. The part I'd spend the most time on with the board, honestly, is the migration itself, because going from zero partitions to this scheme on a 2-billion-row table is the actual risk here. I wouldn't do a big rebuild -- I'd build the new partitioned table alongside the old one, backfill it in batches oldest-first during our quietest windows, and only do a short cutover at the very end for the small sliver of data that's still landing in the old table while we backfill. Validate the numbers match, swap the names, and the outage the business actually feels is minutes, not the hours a full rebuild would cost us.
commonMistakes: Chooses a partition key that doesn't align with both query patterns and maintenance patterns
Proposes daily partitions (too granular, metadata overhead) or yearly partitions (too coarse to switch efficiently) without justifying the choice
Doesn't describe the sliding-window SWITCH mechanism as a metadata-only operation
Proposes migrating via an in-place rebuild of the full table, risking an unacceptable outage at 2 billion rows
Doesn't describe a validation step before cutover, or a plan for the data that lands during the backfill window
keyPoints: Chooses the date key as the partition key, justified by both query and maintenance patterns
Chooses a sensible partition granularity (monthly) with justification
Describes the sliding-window SPLIT/SWITCH mechanism as metadata-only, not row-by-row
Designs a staged, low-outage migration (build alongside, backfill in batches, validate, brief final cutover)
Addresses what happens to in-flight writes during the backfill window

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Chooses and justifies the partition key and granularity
Correctly describes sliding-window maintenance as a metadata-only SWITCH operation
Designs a staged migration that avoids an unacceptable outage at 2 billion rows
Includes a validation step before final cutover

questions.title: Architecture Review: One Centralized Warehouse With Conformed Dimensions, or Federated Per-Department Marts?
questions.prompt: Five departments each want their own data mart, built and owned independently, versus your proposal for one centralized enterprise warehouse with conformed dimensions shared across every subject area. Present both architectures to the review board fairly, then make and defend your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer: Federated per-department marts: each department builds and owns its own dimensional model, independently, on its own timeline, with its own definitions of shared entities like Customer or Product. The genuine advantage is speed and autonomy -- a department isn't blocked waiting on a central team's backlog, and a motivated department can ship value fast. The real cost, which review boards often underweight, is that 'Customer' in Sales and 'Customer' in Finance will drift into incompatible definitions almost immediately without active coordination, and the moment any cross-department question gets asked -- total revenue by customer across both departments' systems -- there's no way to answer it without reconciling two different Customer dimensions after the fact, which is expensive, slow, and a well-documented source of the conflicting-numbers-in-two-reports problem that erodes trust in BI generally. Centralized warehouse with conformed dimensions: every subject area's fact tables reference the same shared dimension tables -- one DimCustomer, one DimProduct, one DimDate -- built once, governed centrally, and reused everywhere, so a query spanning Sales and Finance joins to the same Customer dimension in both cases and the numbers are reconcilable by construction, not by after-the-fact fixing. The cost is real too: a central team becomes a dependency for every department's new subject area, which can genuinely slow down a department that could have moved faster alone, and getting conformed dimension governance right requires real organizational buy-in, not just a technical decision. My recommendation: centralized warehouse with conformed dimensions, but I would not present this as 'no department gets autonomy' -- the Kimball bus architecture pattern this is built on explicitly allows a department to build and own its own fact tables and even department-specific dimensions for things genuinely local to that department, as long as every dimension that's shared across departments (Customer, Product, Date, Employee) is built once, centrally, and conformed. That gives departments real autonomy over their own subject area while guaranteeing that any cross-department question is answerable without reconciliation. I'd propose a lightweight governance process -- a short review before any new shared dimension is created, specifically to catch 'this looks like Customer again' before a sixth version gets built -- rather than a heavy central bottleneck for everything.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay out the federated option honestly, because it does have a real advantage: departments move fast, nobody's waiting on a shared backlog. But I'd be direct about the cost, because it's the cost that actually matters here -- give it six months and Sales' Customer and Finance's Customer won't mean the same thing anymore, and the first time someone asks a cross-department question, we're reconciling two different definitions after the fact instead of just answering the question. That's the exact failure mode that makes two reports show two different numbers for 'the same thing,' and it quietly destroys trust in everything we build after that. My recommendation is the centralized warehouse with conformed dimensions, but I'd push back on anyone hearing that as 'departments lose control.' The Kimball bus architecture this follows explicitly lets a department own its own facts and its own department-specific dimensions -- what has to be shared and governed centrally is only the handful of dimensions that genuinely span departments: Customer, Product, Date, that kind of thing. Built once, conformed, reused everywhere, so a cross-department question is just a query, not a reconciliation project. And I'd keep the governance for that lightweight -- a quick review before anyone builds a new shared dimension, specifically so we catch 'this is just Customer again' early, not a heavyweight bottleneck that makes every department wait on us for everything.
commonMistakes: Presents only one architecture's advantages without fairly describing the other's real tradeoffs
Doesn't name dimension drift / definition incompatibility as the specific, concrete cost of a purely federated approach
Recommends full centralization without acknowledging departments can still own department-specific facts/dimensions under a conformed-dimension model
Proposes heavy central governance for everything instead of a lightweight review scoped to shared dimensions only
Doesn't connect the recommendation to a named, credible architecture pattern (Kimball bus architecture / conformed dimensions)
keyPoints: Fairly presents both federated and centralized architectures with real tradeoffs on each side
Names dimension drift and reconciliation cost as the concrete risk of a purely federated approach
Recommends conformed dimensions while preserving department autonomy over department-specific facts/dimensions
Proposes lightweight, scoped governance rather than a heavy central bottleneck
Grounds the recommendation in a recognized architecture pattern (Kimball bus architecture)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Presents both architectures fairly with genuine tradeoffs
Identifies dimension drift/reconciliation as the concrete cost of federation
Recommends conformed dimensions while preserving appropriate department autonomy
Proposes proportionate, lightweight governance rather than a heavy bottleneck

questions.title: Architecture Review Board: Zero-Downtime Deployment Pipeline Across SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI for a Regulated Client
questions.prompt: A healthcare client needs a formal, auditable deployment pipeline across SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI that satisfies change-control requirements for a regulated industry, while guaranteeing existing production reports and ETL never go down during a release. Design the pipeline end to end, including environment promotion, approval gates, and rollback.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline needs a consistent dev -> test -> prod promotion path across all three tools, with each stage backed by its own environment-specific configuration rather than any hardcoded values, so the exact same deployed artifact behaves correctly as it moves forward: SSIS projects use catalog Environments per stage (Environment Variables mapped per deployment, never a different build per environment); SSRS uses separate Report Server instances or folders per stage with environment-specific data source definitions; Power BI uses separate workspaces per stage (dev/test/prod) with deployment pipelines or a scripted promotion process moving the same .pbix/dataset forward. Approval gates for regulated change control: every promotion from test to prod requires a documented, signed-off change ticket referencing what's being promoted, the test evidence behind it, and who approved it -- this is non-negotiable for audit purposes in a regulated environment, and it has to be enforced structurally (a promotion step that's blocked without an attached approval reference), not just as a verbal policy people are trusted to follow. Zero-downtime guarantee: this is a blue-green-style approach layered onto each tool. For SSIS, the new project version deploys to the catalog alongside the existing one (the catalog supports multiple project versions), and the SQL Agent job triggering the ETL is repointed to the new version only after it's validated, with the prior version retained and ready for immediate rollback. For SSRS, new or changed reports deploy to the server without removing the previous version until validated, and for a changed shared dataset or data source, the change is tested against a non-production copy of the same connection before touching the production data source definition. For Power BI, a new semantic model/report version deploys to a workspace and is validated there before being promoted into the production workspace/app, so end users aren't exposed to an in-progress release; deployment pipelines support exactly this model natively. Rollback: because each stage retains the prior validated version until the new one is confirmed healthy, rollback in every case is 'repoint back to the prior version,' not 'rebuild from scratch,' which keeps rollback time bounded and predictable -- a requirement I'd make explicit to the client, since 'we can roll back in minutes' is itself part of what satisfies a regulated change-control audit.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a regulated client, I'd tell the board up front that this pipeline has two jobs, not one: it has to be auditable, and it has to be safe, and those aren't always the same thing. Auditable means every promotion into production, across all three tools, is tied to a real change ticket with test evidence and a named approver, enforced by the pipeline itself -- not something we trust people to remember to do. Safe means zero downtime, and the way I'd get there is the same pattern in all three tools: never remove the thing that's currently working until the new thing is validated next to it. In SSIS, that's deploying the new project version into the catalog alongside the old one and only repointing the trigger once it's proven; in SSRS, it's deploying new reports or dataset changes without pulling the old ones until they're validated; in Power BI, it's using workspace-based deployment pipelines so a new version proves itself in a non-production workspace before it ever reaches the app end users actually open. And because the old version is never torn down early in any of those, rollback is just 'point back at what was already working,' not an emergency rebuild -- which matters as much to the auditors as it does to me at 2 AM if something goes wrong.
commonMistakes: Designs environment promotion for only one of the three tools and hand-waves the others
Treats change-control approval as a verbal policy instead of a structural gate in the pipeline
Doesn't describe how zero-downtime is actually achieved (retaining the prior version until the new one validates) in each tool
Proposes a rollback plan that amounts to rebuilding from scratch rather than repointing to a retained prior version
Ignores the regulated-industry audit requirement (documented, traceable approvals) as if this were an ordinary deployment
keyPoints: Designs a consistent dev/test/prod promotion path across SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI
Enforces approval gates structurally, with documented, traceable change tickets for audit purposes
Describes a concrete zero-downtime mechanism (retain prior version, validate new version alongside, repoint) for each tool
Designs rollback as a bounded, predictable repoint to a retained prior version
Addresses the regulated-industry audit requirement explicitly, not as an afterthought

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent promotion pipeline across all three tools
Enforces structural, auditable approval gates appropriate for a regulated client
Describes a concrete zero-downtime mechanism per tool
Designs bounded, predictable rollback
