questions.title: Architecture Review: Always On Availability Groups or Failover Clustering for the Platform's SQL Server Engine?
questions.prompt: The SQL Server instance underneath your entire BI platform -- hosting the SSIS catalog, the SSRS report server database, and the warehouse Power BI queries via DirectQuery -- has no high-availability design at all today. Present the Always On Availability Groups vs. failover clustering (FCI) tradeoff to the review board for this specific platform, and make a recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer: Failover Cluster Instances protect the instance by relying on shared storage -- if the active node fails, a passive node takes over the same instance pointed at the same disks, so failover is effectively instantaneous from the data's perspective since there's only one copy of the data. The real limitation for this specific platform is that an FCI protects against server/node failure but not storage failure, since there's exactly one copy of the data on shared storage, and it offers nothing for read-scale -- there's no secondary copy to offload DirectQuery read traffic to, which matters here because Power BI DirectQuery against the warehouse is exactly the kind of read-heavy traffic this platform has to serve. Always On Availability Groups replicate full copies of the databases to one or more secondary replicas, which gives genuine protection against storage failure, not just node failure, since each replica has its own storage, and critically for this platform, a readable secondary can absorb DirectQuery read traffic so reporting load doesn't compete with the SSIS catalog's write-heavy nightly ETL or the SSRS report server database's operational load on the primary. The tradeoff is synchronous vs. asynchronous commit: synchronous commit to a secondary gives zero data loss (RPO zero) but adds write latency, since the primary waits for the secondary to confirm before committing, which can meaningfully slow down a write-heavy nightly ETL window if the secondary is at any distance; asynchronous commit removes that latency cost but accepts some data loss window on failover. My recommendation for this platform specifically: Always On Availability Groups, not FCI, because the read-offload capability directly addresses a real current workload (DirectQuery) that FCI cannot help with at all, and because protecting against storage failure, not just node failure, is a meaningfully stronger guarantee for a platform this central. I'd recommend synchronous commit to a local secondary (for zero-RPO protection against node/storage failure with acceptable latency) plus an asynchronous replica in a second data center for genuine site-level disaster recovery, rather than treating this as a single either-or choice -- the two commit modes solve different problems and a mature design often uses both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this for the board as 'what are we actually trying to protect against, and what else do we get for the same investment.' Failover clustering protects us if a server dies, because a passive node takes over the same shared disks instantly -- but it's still one copy of the data, so a storage failure takes us down anyway, and it gives us nothing extra for the DirectQuery read traffic Power BI is already generating against the warehouse. Always On gives us real copies of the data on separate storage, so we're protected against more than just a dead server, and -- this is the part I'd emphasize -- a readable secondary can actually take that DirectQuery load off the primary, so reporting traffic stops competing with the nightly ETL and the report server's own database load. My recommendation is Always On, specifically because it solves a problem we already have today, not just a hypothetical failure. On commit mode, I wouldn't present it as one choice for everything -- I'd want synchronous commit to a nearby secondary for true zero data loss on a node or storage failure, and an asynchronous replica in a second site for real disaster recovery, because those are genuinely two different problems and trying to solve both with one commit mode means compromising on one of them.
commonMistakes: Recommends FCI without acknowledging it offers no protection against storage failure (single copy of data)
Doesn't connect the recommendation to the platform's actual DirectQuery read-offload need
Presents synchronous vs. asynchronous commit as a single platform-wide choice instead of recognizing they solve different problems (local HA vs. site DR)
Recommends Always On without acknowledging the write-latency cost of synchronous commit on the ETL window
Treats this as a purely technical choice without tying the recommendation to the platform's actual workload
keyPoints: Correctly contrasts FCI (shared storage, node protection only) with Always On (replicated storage, node and storage protection)
Connects the recommendation to the platform's real DirectQuery read-offload need via a readable secondary
Correctly explains the synchronous vs. asynchronous commit tradeoff (RPO vs. write latency)
Recommends a combined approach (synchronous local + asynchronous remote) rather than one commit mode for everything
Grounds the recommendation in this platform's specific workloads, not a generic HA explanation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly contrasts FCI and Always On's actual protection guarantees
Connects the recommendation to the platform's real DirectQuery/read-offload workload
Correctly explains synchronous vs. asynchronous commit tradeoffs
Recommends a coherent, justified HA/DR design for this specific platform

questions.title: Negotiating a Shared Definition of 'Revenue' Between Finance and Sales Leadership
questions.prompt: Finance and Sales leadership both want their own definition of 'Revenue' baked into the same shared semantic model -- Finance wants recognized revenue net of returns and allowances, Sales wants booked revenue at the time of sale. Both insist their number is 'the' revenue number, and both want it labeled simply 'Revenue' with no qualifier. As the architect, how do you resolve this?
questions.modelAnswer: I would not try to arbitrate which definition is 'more correct' -- both are legitimate, well-understood business metrics that answer different real questions, and my job isn't to tell Finance or Sales their definition is wrong. The actual problem is the naming collision, not the metrics themselves: two different, equally valid numbers cannot both be called 'Revenue' with no qualifier in the same model, because every report built afterward inherits that ambiguity and nobody downstream will know which 'Revenue' they're looking at. I'd bring both groups into the same room, show them concretely what happens when an executive pulls up two dashboards built on the same model and sees two different 'Revenue' figures with identical labels -- this isn't hypothetical, it's the standard failure mode that erodes trust in the whole platform -- and propose explicit, unambiguous names for both: 'Booked Revenue' and 'Recognized Revenue' as two separate, clearly documented measures, both available in the same model, neither one hidden or treated as secondary. I'd frame this as giving both groups exactly what they need, correctly labeled, rather than making either side give up their number. If there's residual pressure for an unqualified 'Revenue' somewhere in an executive-level report, I'd push for that report to explicitly state which definition it's using in a visible label or footnote, rather than letting an ambiguous default quietly pick a winner. The result I'm protecting is that any future person looking at either number knows exactly what they're looking at, without having to ask.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to tell either Finance or Sales that their number is wrong, because it isn't -- booked revenue and recognized revenue are both real, legitimate ways to answer different questions, and arguing about which one deserves the plain word 'Revenue' is actually a naming fight, not a metrics fight. So that's how I'd reframe it to both of them, together, in the same room: the problem isn't your number, it's that if we call two different numbers the same thing in the same model, every dashboard anyone builds from here forward is a trap waiting to show two different 'Revenue' figures with the same label, and that's exactly the kind of thing that makes an executive stop trusting the whole platform. My proposal is always to give both groups exactly what they want, just named precisely -- Booked Revenue, Recognized Revenue, both built, both documented, neither one buried as an afterthought. That usually lands fine, because nobody's actually losing their number, they're just not allowed to call it something that conflicts with someone else's equally valid number anymore.
commonMistakes: Tries to decide which definition is 'correct' instead of recognizing both are legitimate for different purposes
Lets both measures ship under the same ambiguous 'Revenue' label to avoid the conflict
Picks one side's definition to end the argument, alienating the other stakeholder group
Doesn't anticipate or address the downstream risk of two differently-labeled dashboards showing conflicting 'Revenue' figures
Treats this as purely a technical naming fix without actually bringing both stakeholder groups into the conversation
keyPoints: Recognizes both definitions as legitimate rather than trying to arbitrate correctness
Reframes the conflict as a naming/governance problem, not a metrics dispute
Proposes explicit, unambiguous names for both measures, both fully supported
Addresses the downstream risk of ambiguous labeling eroding trust in the platform
Resolves the conflict without requiring either stakeholder group to give up their number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes both definitions as legitimate rather than picking a winner
Correctly reframes the conflict as a naming/governance issue
Proposes a concrete resolution (explicit naming) that satisfies both stakeholder groups
Addresses the downstream trust risk of ambiguous metric labeling

questions.title: Leading a Team Through a Contentious Decision: Migrate the Warehouse Now, or Extend the Legacy Platform Two More Years?
questions.prompt: Your team is split roughly in half: some want to start migrating the warehouse to a new platform now, others want to extend the current platform's life for two more years and avoid the migration risk entirely. Both camps feel strongly, and the disagreement is starting to affect team morale. As the lead, how do you run this decision process?
questions.modelAnswer: A split like this usually means the team is arguing from different, unstated assumptions rather than genuinely disagreeing about evidence, so my first move is to get those assumptions onto the table explicitly rather than letting the debate stay at the level of 'migrate now' vs. 'extend.' I'd ask each camp to write down, specifically, what they believe about cost, risk, and timeline -- the migrate-now camp is usually assuming the current platform's technical debt or licensing cost is compounding faster than people realize, and the extend camp is usually assuming the migration risk is higher than the cost of staying put for two more years. Once those are explicit, they're testable: I'd commission a focused, time-boxed spike -- not a full migration, a scoped proof-of-concept against the two or three hardest parts of the real warehouse -- to get actual evidence on migration risk and effort, and pull real numbers on current platform cost trajectory (licensing, support contract renewal timing, known end-of-life dates) rather than letting both camps argue from gut feeling. I'd present the decision to the team as something we're deciding together based on that evidence, not something I'm imposing to settle an argument, and I'd be explicit that whichever way it goes, this isn't a verdict that one camp was 'wrong' -- it's a call made with better information than either side had before. If the decision ultimately goes against what I personally believe going in, I'd still make and own it based on the evidence rather than my prior opinion. The thing I'd watch for afterward is whether the camp that didn't get their preferred outcome actually buys in or just goes quiet -- so I'd follow up individually with people who seemed most invested in the other direction, not just announce the decision and move on.
questions.professionalAnswer: When a team splits roughly in half on something like this, my experience is that it's rarely really about the conclusion -- it's about different unstated assumptions nobody's actually tested. So I don't try to referee the argument as it's being had; I ask both camps to write down specifically what they believe is true about cost, risk, and timeline, because once that's explicit, we can actually go check it instead of debating gut feelings. Usually that means a scoped, time-boxed spike against the hardest two or three parts of our actual warehouse to get real migration-risk data, plus real numbers on what staying on the current platform is actually costing us and when real deadlines like end-of-life or contract renewal actually land. I bring the decision back to the team with that evidence and frame it as something we're deciding together, not something I'm using to declare one side the winner, because that framing matters a lot for whether the camp that didn't get their way actually buys in afterward or just quietly checks out. And honestly, if the evidence points the other way from where I started, I'll say so and go with it -- the decision has to be about what we actually learned, not about who argued harder in the room.
commonMistakes: Settles the debate by personal authority or gut feeling instead of surfacing and testing the underlying assumptions
Lets the team keep arguing from opinion without commissioning any actual evidence (cost data, a scoped technical spike)
Frames the eventual decision as one camp winning and the other losing, instead of a shared, evidence-based call
Doesn't follow up individually with people most invested in the outcome that didn't happen, risking silent disengagement
Makes the decision match their own prior opinion regardless of what the evidence actually shows
keyPoints: Surfaces each camp's unstated assumptions about cost, risk, and timeline explicitly
Commissions real evidence (a scoped technical spike, actual cost/timeline data) rather than deciding on opinion
Frames the decision as a shared, evidence-based call rather than one side winning an argument
Remains willing to be moved by the evidence even against a prior personal opinion
Follows up individually with the camp that didn't get its preferred outcome to confirm real buy-in

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Surfaces underlying assumptions rather than treating this as a simple two-sided debate
Proposes concrete, real evidence-gathering (spike, cost data) before deciding
Frames the decision as shared and evidence-based rather than a win/loss outcome
Addresses follow-up with the camp that didn't get its preferred outcome

questions.title: Owning the Postmortem After a Botched Catalog Deployment Took Down Nightly Loads for a Full Business Day
questions.prompt: A deployment to the SSIS catalog went wrong during a routine release window, and nightly ETL loads were down for a full business day before the team fully diagnosed and fixed it. You're leading the postmortem. Walk through how you run it and what comes out of it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start the postmortem by being explicit about what it is and isn't: a blameless, factual reconstruction of what happened and why, aimed at fixing the process that allowed it, not an exercise in identifying who to blame -- and I'd say that out loud at the start, because people self-censor the details that actually matter if they think the meeting is building a case against them. I'd build the actual timeline first, with real timestamps -- when the deployment ran, when the first failure was detected, when it was escalated, when root cause was identified, when the fix deployed -- because a full business day of downtime almost always contains more than one failure, not just the original deployment issue: there's usually also a detection gap (how long before anyone noticed) and an escalation gap (how long before the right person was actually working the problem), and each of those gaps is a separate, fixable thing. Root cause: whatever specifically went wrong in the deployment itself -- a missing environment mapping, an untested parameter change, whatever the actual technical cause turns out to be -- gets named precisely, not vaguely. Then I'd walk through each gap and ask, for each one, what concrete process change would have caught or shortened it: if detection took hours, that's a monitoring/alerting gap, and the fix is an automated check on nightly load completion, not 'be more vigilant'; if escalation took too long, that's an on-call/runbook gap, and the fix is a documented escalation path, not 'communicate better.' I'd insist every action item from this postmortem have a named owner and a date, because a postmortem that ends with a list of vague intentions and no accountability is the single most common way a real incident fails to produce any lasting improvement. I'd also push for whatever specific deployment-time check would have caught this particular failure to become a mandatory step in every future release, not an optional best practice people are trusted to remember.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I say out loud when I open a postmortem like this is that we're not here to find out whose fault it is -- we're here to find out exactly what happened and fix the process that let it happen, because if people think this meeting is building a case against someone, I lose all the honest detail I actually need. So I build a real timeline first, with actual timestamps, because a full day of downtime is almost never just one failure -- there's the original deployment problem, but there's also however long it took anyone to notice, and however long it took to get the right person actually working it, and those are two separate, fixable gaps on top of the technical root cause. For each gap, I push the room past 'we should communicate better' and toward something specific and ownable -- if detection was slow, that's an alerting gap and the fix is an automated check, not a reminder to pay closer attention; if escalation was slow, that's a documented on-call path, not a vague promise. And every single action item coming out of that meeting gets a name and a date next to it, because I've seen plenty of postmortems produce a good conversation and zero actual change, and the difference is always whether anyone's accountable for the follow-through.
commonMistakes: Runs the postmortem in a way that feels like assigning blame, causing people to self-censor important details
Treats the incident as one single failure instead of separating the root cause from detection and escalation gaps
Proposes vague fixes ('communicate better', 'be more careful') instead of concrete process or tooling changes
Doesn't assign a named owner and date to each action item
Doesn't make the specific check that would have caught this failure a mandatory future release step
keyPoints: Frames the postmortem explicitly as blameless and fact-finding, not blame-assigning
Builds a real timeline separating root cause, detection gap, and escalation gap as distinct, separately-fixable issues
Converts vague intentions into concrete, specific process or tooling fixes
Assigns a named owner and date to every action item
Makes the specific preventive check a mandatory step in future releases, not an optional best practice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames the postmortem as blameless and factual
Separates root cause from detection and escalation gaps as distinct issues
Converts findings into concrete, ownable action items with dates
Proposes making the preventive fix mandatory going forward

questions.title: Telling a VP Their Requested Real-Time Dashboard Isn't Feasible on the Current Architecture
questions.prompt: A VP asks for a dashboard that updates in real time as transactions happen. Your current architecture refreshes the semantic model on a scheduled basis and genuinely cannot do sub-second real-time updates without a significant redesign the VP hasn't budgeted for. How do you handle this conversation without just saying no?
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't open with 'that's not possible,' because that's technically imprecise and it closes the conversation instead of moving it forward -- what's actually true is that true real-time isn't feasible on the current architecture without a redesign that isn't currently budgeted, which is a very different, more useful statement. My first move is to understand what the VP is actually trying to solve, because 'real time' is often a proxy for a specific pain -- usually 'I'm making decisions on numbers that are too stale,' not literally 'I need sub-second latency.' Once I understand the real need, I'd lay out the honest spectrum of options with their actual cost and latency tradeoffs: the current scheduled refresh (cheap, but however stale the current interval is), a shorter scheduled refresh interval (cheap incremental improvement, still not real-time), DirectQuery against the source for near-real-time numbers at the cost of some query performance and load on the source system, and a genuine real-time architecture (streaming ingestion, a fundamentally different pipeline) that solves the stated request literally but requires a scoped project with its own budget and timeline. I'd recommend whichever point on that spectrum actually matches the business problem the VP described, not necessarily the most technically impressive option, and I'd be explicit that if what they actually need is 'every 15 minutes instead of nightly,' we might be able to deliver real business value cheaply and quickly, without needing the full real-time rebuild they initially asked for by name. This turns 'no' into 'here's what's actually achievable at what cost, and here's what I'd recommend for the problem you're describing,' which gives the VP a real decision to make instead of a wall.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never want to just tell a VP 'no' to this, because it's not actually true and it ends the conversation instead of helping them. What's true is that sub-second real-time isn't something our current architecture does without a redesign nobody's budgeted for -- so instead of leading with the limitation, I lead with a question: what's the actual decision you're trying to make faster, because 'real time' is usually standing in for 'I'm looking at numbers that are too old for what I need to decide,' not literally millisecond freshness. Once I know that, I can lay out the real menu: our current refresh schedule, a tighter refresh interval that's a cheap change, DirectQuery for something close to real-time with a real performance tradeoff on the source system, or an actual real-time pipeline if they genuinely need that and are willing to scope and fund it as its own project. Most of the time, what actually solves their problem is something much cheaper than full real-time, and I'd rather hand them that option clearly than either say no or quietly over-promise something we can't deliver on the current budget.
commonMistakes: Simply says the request isn't possible without exploring what the VP is actually trying to solve
Over-promises real-time capability to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, setting up a later failure
Doesn't present the real spectrum of options (refresh interval, DirectQuery, true real-time) with honest tradeoffs
Recommends the most technically impressive option rather than the one that actually fits the underlying business need
Frames the conversation as a technical limitation rather than a cost/timeline/scope conversation the VP can actually decide on
keyPoints: Avoids a flat 'no,' instead clarifying the real underlying business need behind the request
Presents an honest spectrum of real options with their actual cost/latency tradeoffs
Recommends the option that fits the actual underlying need, not the most impressive-sounding one
Reframes the conversation as a scoped decision the VP can make, not a technical wall
Doesn't over-promise a capability the current architecture can't deliver

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids a flat refusal, instead exploring the VP's actual underlying need
Presents a real, honest spectrum of options with tradeoffs
Recommends an option matched to the real need rather than over- or under-selling
Frames the conversation as a decision for the VP rather than a technical dead end

questions.title: Rolling Out Mandatory Code Review for SSIS and DAX Changes to a Team That's Never Had One
questions.prompt: Your team of five BI developers has shipped SSIS packages and Power BI models for years with no code review process at all -- changes go straight from a developer's machine to production. You want to introduce mandatory review before anything ships. How do you roll this out without it landing as a vote of no confidence in a team that's been shipping successfully?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd be careful about the framing from the very first conversation, because 'I'm adding review because you've been making mistakes' is both untrue and exactly the message a team that's shipped successfully for years will hear if I'm not deliberate about this. I'd ground the change in a specific, real incident or near-miss if one exists -- 'this is the kind of thing a second set of eyes catches before it reaches production, not after' -- rather than presenting it as a generic best practice imposed from above, because a concrete example makes the reasoning visible instead of abstract. I'd roll it out gradually rather than as a single mandatory policy on day one: start with review as encouraged-but-optional for a short period, let the team experience a few real catches (even small ones) firsthand, and use those as the case for making it mandatory, so the team arrives at 'yes, this is worth doing' through their own experience rather than a mandate handed down. I'd also make the review process itself lightweight and fast -- a quick structured checklist for an SSIS package or DAX change, not a heavyweight gate that makes every release noticeably slower -- because if review becomes a bottleneck, the team's resentment will be aimed at the process, not the goal, and that resentment is exactly what undermines a change like this long-term. I'd rotate who reviews whom rather than making it always flow one direction, so it reads as a shared team practice everyone participates in, not scrutiny applied downward from the lead onto developers.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'm careful with how I open this conversation, because if I lead with 'we're adding review,' a team that's been shipping fine for years hears 'you don't trust us anymore,' and that's not what I mean and not what's true. So I'd ground it in something concrete if I have it -- a specific near-miss or a specific bug that review would have caught before it reached production -- because that makes the case visible instead of abstract. And I wouldn't flip the switch to mandatory on day one. I'd start with review as something people can opt into, let the team actually experience a few real catches for themselves, and let that experience build the case rather than me building it for them. I'd also make sure review itself stays fast and lightweight -- a short checklist, not a heavy gate -- because the fastest way to make a team resent a good process is to let it slow every release down noticeably. And I'd rotate who reviews whom, so it feels like something the whole team does together, not something I'm imposing on everyone else from above.
commonMistakes: Frames the new process as a response to the team's past mistakes, reading as a vote of no confidence
Mandates the full process immediately instead of letting the team experience its value gradually
Designs a heavyweight review process that visibly slows down every release
Makes review flow one direction only (lead reviewing everyone), reading as scrutiny rather than a shared practice
Rolls the change out with no concrete example of what it would have caught, keeping the justification abstract
keyPoints: Avoids framing the change as a response to the team's past failures
Grounds the change in a concrete example where possible
Rolls the process out gradually, letting the team experience its value before making it mandatory
Keeps the review process lightweight so it doesn't visibly slow down releases
Rotates reviewers so the practice reads as shared, not scrutiny applied downward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids framing the change as distrust of the team's past work
Proposes a gradual rollout that builds buy-in through experience
Designs a lightweight process that doesn't become a release bottleneck
Proposes a structure (rotation) that reads as shared practice, not top-down scrutiny

questions.title: Standardizing on Power BI When a Department Built Its Own Shadow BI System in Excel and Access
questions.prompt: Leadership wants to standardize all BI on Power BI, retiring ad hoc reporting. One department has, over several years, built an elaborate shadow system of linked Excel workbooks and an Access database that they rely on daily and are genuinely attached to. How do you lead the migration of that department without alienating them or losing what actually works about their system?
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct to walk in and declare the shadow system a problem to be eliminated is exactly how this goes wrong -- that system exists and has survived for years because it's actually solving real problems for that department, even if it's also creating real risk (no version control, fragile linked-workbook dependencies, no audit trail, single points of failure if the one person who understands the Access database leaves). My first move is to actually understand what it does well before proposing to replace it: sit with the department, have them walk me through their real workflow, and identify specifically which parts of their process the shadow system is genuinely serving -- flexibility to slice data in ways central tools haven't supported, speed, a sense of ownership over their own numbers -- versus which parts are pure risk with no corresponding benefit. I'd frame the migration explicitly as 'let's build you something that does everything this does, plus removes the risk you're carrying,' not 'stop using what you built because it's against policy.' I'd involve department staff directly in designing the Power BI replacement, specifically because the people who built and maintained the shadow system understand the real business logic buried in those workbooks better than anyone else, and treating them as the experts on their own domain during the build protects their sense of ownership instead of stripping it away. I'd migrate in parallel, not cut over abruptly -- keep the shadow system running until the new Power BI solution has been validated against it for a real stretch of time, so the department never has to trust a new system on faith while their own livelihood depends on the numbers being right. The policy goal (standardize on Power BI) and the department's real need (a system that actually works for their specific workflow) aren't in conflict if I do this right -- they only look like they're in conflict if I lead with the policy instead of the workflow.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I'd be most careful to avoid is walking in and treating their system as the problem, because from their side, it's not a problem -- it's something they built and have relied on for years because it actually works for them, even if it's also a real risk from where I sit. So I start by actually learning it: sit with them, have them walk me through their real day-to-day with it, and figure out specifically what it's doing right for them versus what's just risk with no upside -- no version control, no audit trail, one person who understands the Access database and nobody else. Then I frame the migration as addition, not subtraction: we're building something that does everything their system does for them, and also removes the risk they've been quietly carrying. I bring their own people into designing the Power BI replacement, because they understand the real business logic in those workbooks better than I ever will, and that involvement is also what keeps this from feeling like something being done to them. And I run the two side by side for a real stretch of time rather than cutting over on a deadline, because I'm not going to ask them to trust a new system with numbers their job depends on until it's actually proven itself against the thing they already trust.
commonMistakes: Treats the shadow system as simply wrong or against policy without understanding what it's actually solving for the department
Mandates an abrupt cutover instead of running the new system in parallel until it's proven
Excludes department staff from designing the replacement, losing the real business logic embedded in their existing system
Frames the migration purely as policy compliance rather than addressing the department's real workflow needs
Doesn't acknowledge the genuine risk in the shadow system (no audit trail, single point of failure) as the actual justification for change
keyPoints: Starts by understanding what the shadow system actually does well for the department, not just its risks
Frames the migration as addition (same capability, less risk) rather than pure removal of what they built
Involves department staff directly in designing the replacement to capture real business logic and preserve ownership
Runs the new and old systems in parallel until the replacement is genuinely validated
Balances the organizational governance goal with the department's genuine, legitimate workflow needs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Understands and respects what the shadow system is actually solving before proposing change
Frames the migration as addition rather than punitive removal
Involves department staff in designing the replacement
Proposes a parallel-run migration rather than an abrupt cutover

questions.title: A DR Tabletop Exercise Reveals Your Disaster Recovery Plan Can't Actually Meet the RTO You Promised
questions.prompt: You run a disaster-recovery tabletop exercise for the BI platform, and it reveals that the documented recovery process would actually take roughly 10 hours -- well past the 4-hour RTO leadership believes the platform has. Walk through how you handle discovering this, communicating it upward, and fixing it.
questions.modelAnswer: The moment this gap surfaces in the tabletop, my first instinct is not to quietly fix the documentation or the plan before anyone outside the exercise finds out -- that's the natural, understandable urge, and it's exactly the wrong move, because leadership is currently making real decisions (what they'd tell customers, regulators, or the board during an actual outage) based on a 4-hour number that isn't true. I'd treat discovering this as good news in disguise -- better to find it in a tabletop than during a real incident -- and communicate it upward promptly and honestly: here's what the exercise found, here's the real current recovery time, here's why the gap exists, and here's the plan to close it, all in one conversation rather than leading with just the bad news and leaving people to assume the worst or, alternately, downplaying it to avoid an uncomfortable conversation. I'd be specific about why the gap exists -- usually a tabletop surfaces something like a manual step that was assumed to be automated, a dependency on a person who might not be reachable, or a restore procedure that was never actually tested end-to-end at realistic scale -- because 'the RTO is wrong' is much less useful to leadership than 'here specifically is what's actually slow, and here's what closing that gap requires.' Then I'd propose a concrete remediation plan with its own timeline and, if closing the gap requires investment leadership hasn't budgeted (more automation, a faster backup/restore mechanism, additional tooling), I'd be explicit that the choice is between funding the fix or formally revising the RTO commitment to match reality -- I would not let the organization keep operating on a stated number everyone now knows is false, because that's a decision nobody's actually making, it's just happening by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: The instinct I'd have to fight is wanting to quietly fix this before anyone finds out, because that feels safer in the moment but it's actually the wrong call -- leadership is making real decisions right now based on a 4-hour number, and if it's actually 10, they need to know that before it matters, not after. So I treat finding this in a tabletop as exactly what the exercise is for -- better here than in a real incident -- and I go to leadership promptly with the full picture in one conversation: here's what we found, here's the real number, here's specifically why it's not 4 hours, and here's what I'd propose to close the gap. I'm specific about the why, because 'the RTO is wrong' isn't actionable, but 'this manual step we assumed was automated is actually the bottleneck' is something we can actually go fix. And if closing that gap costs money or time nobody's budgeted, I say that plainly too -- the actual decision in front of leadership is fund the fix or officially change the number we're promising, and I'm not going to let us keep quietly operating on a number everyone in the room now knows isn't true.
commonMistakes: Quietly fixes the gap before reporting it, leaving leadership making decisions on a false RTO in the meantime
Reports the finding vaguely ('our DR plan needs work') without specifying the real recovery time and why the gap exists
Downplays the severity of the gap to avoid an uncomfortable conversation with leadership
Doesn't present a concrete remediation plan, or doesn't frame the real choice (fund the fix vs. revise the RTO commitment)
Treats finding the gap as a failure to hide rather than exactly what the exercise was designed to surface
keyPoints: Reports the finding promptly and honestly rather than quietly fixing it first
Communicates the specific real recovery time and the specific reason for the gap
Frames discovering the gap in a tabletop as a success of the exercise, not a failure to conceal
Proposes a concrete remediation plan with its own timeline
Presents the real choice to leadership explicitly: fund the fix or formally revise the RTO commitment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Reports the gap promptly and honestly rather than concealing or delaying it
Communicates specific, actionable detail about why the gap exists
Proposes a concrete remediation plan
Frames the real decision for leadership (fund the fix vs. revise the commitment)

questions.title: Mediating Two Senior Engineers Who Disagree in Front of the Team Over Star vs. Snowflake Schema
questions.prompt: Two senior engineers on your team get into a visible, somewhat heated disagreement in a design meeting over whether a new subject area should use a star schema or a snowflake schema, and neither is backing down in front of the rest of the team. As the lead, how do you handle the moment and the underlying decision?
questions.modelAnswer: In the moment, my first job is de-escalation, not resolution -- two senior people digging in publicly isn't actually about to produce a good technical decision, it's going to produce a winner and a loser in front of the team, which damages both relationships and the team's trust that disagreements get handled well here. I'd interrupt constructively: acknowledge that this is a real, legitimate design question worth getting right, and move it out of the open meeting into a focused follow-up with just the two of them and me, rather than litigating it live in front of everyone who doesn't need to watch two senior engineers posture at each other. In that follow-up, I'd get both of their actual reasoning on the table -- star schema's query simplicity and performance versus snowflake's reduced redundancy and more precise handling of a specific hierarchy -- because at the senior level, both positions are usually defensible engineering opinions, not one obviously right and one obviously wrong, and treating it that way from the start keeps both people engaged rather than defensive. I'd push for the decision to be grounded in the actual characteristics of this specific subject area -- how deep and how stable is the hierarchy in question, what do the real query patterns against it look like, is storage or redundancy actually a meaningful cost here -- rather than either engineer's general preference, because a decision grounded in this subject area's specifics is more defensible to both of them than 'my opinion beats your opinion.' Once decided, I'd document the reasoning (an ADR-style record) so it's clear this was a reasoned call based on specific tradeoffs, not just whoever outlasted the other. Afterward, I'd address the public dynamic separately and privately with both of them -- not to relitigate who was right, but because a repeat of a heated public disagreement is a team-health problem I need to head off regardless of who was technically correct this time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The public moment is the thing I handle first, before the actual schema question, because two senior people digging in in front of the team isn't going anywhere good live -- somebody's about to look like they lost in public, and that costs more than whatever we gain from settling it in the room. So I interrupt, I say this is a real question worth getting right, and I take it offline to the three of us rather than letting it play out as a spectator event. Once it's just us, I want to actually hear both arguments in full, because at this level it's rarely one obviously right answer and one obviously wrong one -- star schema's simplicity and performance against snowflake's reduced redundancy for a genuinely deep, stable hierarchy are both real engineering positions. I push the conversation toward the specifics of this subject area -- how the hierarchy actually behaves, what the real query patterns look like -- because grounding the decision in this case, not in either person's general philosophy, is something both of them can actually accept even if it's not their first choice. I write down the reasoning so it's clearly a reasoned call, not a coin flip or whoever talked longer. And separately, I'd talk to both of them privately about the public disagreement itself, because that's a team dynamic I need to address regardless of who ends up being right about schemas.
commonMistakes: Lets the disagreement play out live in the meeting instead of moving it to a focused follow-up
Picks a side quickly just to end the public conflict, without grounding the decision in the subject area's actual characteristics
Treats one engineer's position as obviously correct and the other as obviously wrong instead of recognizing both as defensible
Doesn't document the reasoning behind the eventual decision
Addresses only the technical question and ignores the team-health issue of a heated public disagreement
keyPoints: De-escalates the public moment by moving the disagreement to a focused follow-up conversation
Treats both senior engineers' positions as legitimate engineering viewpoints rather than picking an obvious winner
Grounds the final decision in the specific subject area's characteristics rather than either engineer's general preference
Documents the decision's reasoning for future reference
Separately addresses the public dynamic as a team-health issue, independent of the technical outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: De-escalates the public moment appropriately
Treats both positions as legitimate and gathers full reasoning from each
Grounds the decision in the specific subject area's characteristics
Addresses the team-health dynamic separately from the technical decision

questions.title: Negotiating Sequencing With Three Regional Stakeholder Groups Who All Want to Go First
questions.prompt: You're migrating three regional business units onto a new centralized reporting platform. All three regional VPs insist their region must be migrated first, each with their own business justification. You have resources to migrate one region at a time. How do you negotiate the sequencing without any region feeling deprioritized or ignored?
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct to avoid is picking a sequence privately and then announcing it, because however well-reasoned it is, it will land as arbitrary to the two regions that didn't go first, and arbitrary-feeling decisions are what actually damage trust, not the sequencing outcome itself. I'd bring all three VPs into the same conversation, not three separate ones, and establish shared, objective sequencing criteria before discussing any specific region -- things like current risk exposure on the legacy system, size and complexity of the migration, dependency relationships between regions (does one region's data feed another's reports), and genuine business urgency with real evidence behind it, not just who argues most forcefully. I'd ask each VP to make their case against those shared criteria, in front of the others, which does two things: it keeps the conversation about the criteria rather than politics, and it means whichever region goes first is seen to have earned it against a standard everyone agreed to, not been handed it by me. I'd be explicit that 'migrating second or third' doesn't mean deprioritized -- I'd commit to and publish a real timeline for all three regions, not just the first one, so the second and third regions have a concrete date to hold me to rather than an open-ended 'eventually.' And I'd look for any genuine technical dependency that makes the sequencing decision partly made for us -- if one region's data structure needs to exist before another's reports can be built correctly, that's a legitimate, non-political reason for an order that I can point to, which is more defensible than relative urgency alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I wouldn't do is sequence this myself behind closed doors and then announce it, because no matter how good my reasoning is, the two regions that didn't go first are going to read it as arbitrary, and that's the thing that actually costs me trust with them going forward. So I get all three VPs in one room, not three separate conversations, and before anyone argues for their own region, we agree on the criteria together -- current risk on the legacy system, migration complexity, any real dependency between regions, genuine urgency backed by actual evidence. Then each VP makes their case against those shared criteria, in front of each other, which keeps it about the criteria instead of who can push hardest in a one-on-one with me. And I make sure going second or third doesn't mean waiting in the dark -- I commit to a real published timeline for all three up front, so nobody's stuck with an open-ended 'we'll get to you.' If there's an actual technical dependency that partly decides the order for us, I use that, because 'this has to happen first because of how the data actually works' is a much easier thing for everyone to accept than 'I decided your region matters less right now.'
commonMistakes: Decides the sequencing privately and announces it without involving all three stakeholder groups in the criteria
Uses vague or inconsistent criteria, making the eventual sequence look political rather than principled
Doesn't communicate a concrete timeline for the regions migrating second and third, leaving them with an open-ended wait
Picks whichever VP argued most forcefully rather than evaluating against shared, objective criteria
Ignores genuine technical dependencies between regions that could partly determine a defensible order

questions.title: Leading the Process Fix After an 'Emergency' Change Bypassed the Review Gate
questions.prompt: During a late-night production issue, an engineer bypassed your mandatory change-review gate to push a fix directly, calling it an emergency. The fix actually introduced a second, worse problem. Walk through how you handle the engineer, the immediate cleanup, and the process itself afterward.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd separate three things that are easy to collapse into one angry conversation: the immediate cleanup, how I handle the engineer, and what's actually wrong with the process. Cleanup comes first and is purely technical -- diagnose and fix the second problem the bypassed change introduced, with the same urgency as the original issue, before anything else. On the engineer: I would not treat this primarily as a discipline problem, because the more important question is why bypassing the gate felt like the right call to someone at 2 AM under pressure -- did they not know how to invoke an emergency-change process that exists but is slower than just pushing the fix, did no emergency path exist at all so bypassing felt like the only option, or did they understand the gate and consciously decide the rule didn't apply to them. Those are three very different problems with three different fixes, and I'd have that conversation directly and calmly with the engineer to find out which one it actually was, rather than assuming. If it's the first two, the real failure is organizational -- we don't have a legitimate fast path for genuine emergencies, so people invent their own -- and the fix is building one: a real emergency-change process that's fast but still requires a second set of eyes, even a quick verbal sign-off from one other engineer, rather than nothing at all. If it's genuinely the third case, that's a more serious conversation about judgment and trust, but I'd still want to understand it fully before concluding that. Either way, the process fix I'd push hardest for is making the legitimate path faster and clearer than the workaround, because a review gate that's slower than bypassing it will always eventually get bypassed under enough pressure -- that's a design flaw in the gate, not just a discipline failure in the person who went around it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep three things separate in my head here, because mixing them together turns this into one bad conversation instead of three useful ones. First, pure cleanup -- fix the second problem the bypass caused, with the same urgency we'd give any production issue, before I worry about anything else. Second, the conversation with the engineer, which I don't walk into assuming it's a discipline issue. I actually want to know why bypassing the gate felt like the right call at 2 AM -- did they not know there was supposed to be a faster emergency path, was there genuinely no fast path and they improvised one, or did they know the rule and decide it didn't apply to them right then. Those are really different situations. Third, and this is usually where I end up spending the most energy: if there's no legitimate fast path for a real emergency, that's on the process, not on the engineer, and I need to build one -- fast, but still with at least one other set of eyes, even a quick verbal check-in, not zero oversight. Because if the official path is slower than just going around it, people will keep going around it under enough pressure, no matter how many times I tell them not to -- that's a flaw in the gate, and fixing that is more valuable than being angry at the one person who happened to hit it first.
